sens: native or treated gold to achieve maximum purity
characteristic color and luster of this refined gold
supreme quality, excellence
symbol of priceless value and beauty
H3800.detail:
1. The Hebrew word kétem specifically refers to gold in its purest and most refined form — either native gold found in nature or gold that has been worked and purified to remove impurities. It is gold of exceptional quality, as seen in Job 28:16 where pure gold is paralleled with other precious treasures, and in Job 28:19 which emphasizes its unmatched value.

2. This pure gold shines with a characteristic luster, an intense golden color that makes it immediately recognizable. In Song of Solomon 5:11, the beloved's hair is described as black "like a raven," but interspersed with reflections that evoke this resplendent pure gold.

3. Beyond its market value, pure gold represents what is best and most excellent. In Proverbs 25:12, a wise word addressed to the listener is compared to a ring or a jewel of pure gold — indicating that wisdom, like pure gold, is infinitely precious.

4. Pure gold becomes a biblical image of what is invaluable, irreplaceable, worthy of supreme respect. In Lamentations 4:1, the precious sons of Zion are compared to pure gold bars — showing that nothing can rival their value, not even the most refined gold.
H3800.origine: The word kétem comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of purification and refinement. It is related to other Hebrew words denoting precious metals and specifically deals with gold in its state of maximum purity. The basic image is that of a metal that has been purified, free from any stain or imperfection — hence its figurative use to denote excellence and perfection.
H3800.emploi: The word kétem appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the Wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs, Song of Solomon) and in the prophets (Isaiah, Daniel). In Job 28, in the context of the search for wisdom, pure gold is presented as an incomparable treasure in value and difficulty of acquisition. In Proverbs 25:12, it illustrates the beauty of wise words. The Song of Solomon uses it to evoke physical beauty (hair, skin color). Isaiah 13:12 uses it in an eschatological perspective: humans will become rarer than pure gold on the day of judgment. Daniel 10:5 places it on the chest of a heavenly vision, marking holiness and superhuman splendor. Lamentations 4:1 uses it to amplify the tragedy of the destruction of Jerusalem.
H3800.portee: Pure gold in the Bible is never just a commodity: it is the image of what is absolutely precious, incorruptible, and worthy of desire. For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God alone is more precious than pure gold — which is why wisdom, the word of God, and true beauty are measured by this scale of value. It invites us to distinguish what is truly precious (wisdom, justice, the people of God) from what only has the appearance of treasure.

sens: Undergarment, usually made of linen, worn directly on the skin
Priestly garment, part of the liturgical uniform of the priests of Israel
Garment of honor or dignity worn by important figures
H3801.detail:
1. The tunic is a basic garment, a kind of long shirt made of fine fabric (often linen) that is worn over the body. It is an undergarment in the hierarchy of clothing: it is put on first, then other pieces are added over it. When God clothes Adam and Eve in Genesis 3:21, He makes them "garments of skin," which are also referred to as tunics — the basic garment to cover the body.
2. In worship, the priestly tunic is an official and ritually prescribed garment: it clothes the one who approaches God to serve Him. In Exodus 28:40 and Leviticus 16:4, the sons of Aaron and the high priest must wear a white linen tunic before performing their duties. It is a marker of their status and consecration.
3. A finely woven or remarkably colored tunic becomes a badge of social rank or honor. The "coat of many colors" that Jacob gives to Joseph in Genesis 37:3 is an exceptional garment that provokes the jealousy of his brothers — it signals that Joseph is the favored child, clothed in dignity.
H3801.origine: The Hebrew word kuttoneth (קֻתֹּנֶת) refers to a very ancient garment from the Near East. Its exact etymology is debated, but it may be related to a root that evokes the idea of wrapping or covering. It is a common word throughout the Hebrew Bible and in ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts, indicating that the tunic was the ordinary garment of all the peoples of the Levant — a universal and basic garment.
H3801.emploi: The word kuttoneth appears 26 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Torah (Genesis and Exodus) and in the historical books. It is used in three distinct contexts: first as an ordinary garment and covering for the body (Genesis 3:21, Job 30:18); second as a priestly uniform precisely prescribed by the Law (Exodus 28, Leviticus 8, Leviticus 16); and finally as a mark of status or honor (Genesis 37:3, 2 Samuel 13:18, Isaiah 22:21). Prophets and kings also wear dignifying tunics. The context always indicates whether one is speaking of the simple garment of the poor or the rich, of the sacred official or the civil.
H3801.portee: The tunic reminds us that our clothing is not a detail: it covers our nakedness, marks our place in society, and — when it comes to serving God — requires respectful preparation. Consider the high priest's tunic, white as snow (Leviticus 16:4), a symbol of purity before entering the presence of the Holy One: even our clothes should reflect our intention and faith when we approach God.

sens: Part of the human body between the neck and the arm
Part of an animal's body used for carrying or pulling
Piece of clothing or armor covering the shoulder
Side or edge of a surface, a mountain
Support or bracket serving as a prop
H3802.detail:
1. The shoulder is the part of the human body that connects the arm to the torso. It is an important joint allowing for arm movement. The Bible mentions it notably when carrying something: the Levites carry the ark of God on their shoulders with poles (1 Chronicles 15:15), and fathers will bring the children of Israel on their shoulders (Isaiah 49:22).
2. In animals, the shoulder also refers to this same anatomical region, used for carrying burdens. The shoulders of the animal support what is placed on its back.
3. The shoulder piece or epaulet is a piece of fabric or metal attached to the shoulder, serving as an ornament or protection. On the high priest's ephod, engraved stones were placed on the shoulder pieces to remember the sons of Israel (Exodus 39:7).
4. In a geographical context, the side or shoulder of a mountain or region refers to its slope or flank. For example, a boundary runs along the northern side facing Araba (Joshua 18:18).
5. A bracket or support is an architectural piece that protrudes to support a structure: the brackets of the altars or basins of the temple function as supports under the objects placed on them.
H3802.origine: The Hebrew word כָּתֵף (kateph) comes from a root meaning to carry or to support. It belongs to a family of words describing elements that support or carry something. The term first applies to the body (human or animal), and then by extension to architectural structures that fulfill a similar function: to support, carry, maintain.
H3802.emploi: This word appears 58 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books and the prophets. Its usage varies according to context: in Leviticus and Exodus, it describes the shoulder pieces of the priestly ephod and the parts of the ark of the covenant (Exodus 39:7). In the historical books (Joshua, Kings, Chronicles), it regularly designates the flank or side of a mountain or region in boundary descriptions. In the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel), it expresses both the physical action of carrying (Isaiah 49:22) and metaphorical images of strength or support. The word is also used for furniture pieces in the temple (brackets of the basins).
H3802.portee: The shoulder in the Bible often symbolizes strength and the ability to bear a burden. When God says He will raise His banner to the peoples and they will carry the children of Israel on their shoulders, it expresses powerful support and victory. Similarly, the carrying of the ark on the shoulders of the Levites shows their sacred responsibility in serving God. This word also reminds us that our physical strength is at the service of a calling that transcends us.

sens: Place someone or something at the center, encircling it from all sides
Wait, stay close to someone in expectation
Carry as an ornament or mark of distinction
Dominate, triumph over
Festoon or border
H3803.detail: 1. To place at the center by encircling: this is the most concrete image. Soldiers surround Benjamin, pressing in on him until they crush him (Judges 20:43). Wild bulls surround the psalmist, encircling him like predators (Psalms 22:13). The righteous will come to surround him when God has acted for him (Psalms 142:8). 2. To wait, stay in expectation: the word can also mean "to stay close to" or "to wait for" someone. Job says to Bildad: "Wait a moment, and I will continue" (Job 36:2), as if the word retains the idea of patient proximity. 3. To carry as an adornment or symbol: figuratively, wisdom forms a crown for the prudent man (Proverbs 14:18), adorning and distinguishing the one who possesses it. 4. To dominate or triumph: the wicked "triumphs" over the righteous (Habakkuk 1:4), the idea of encircling transforming into that of surpassing or victory.
H3803.origine: The Hebrew verb כָּתַר comes from a root that first evokes the idea of surrounding, forming a crown or circle around something. The same root produces the word כֶּתֶר (kétèr), "crown" — that which turns, that which encircles. The image is that of a band, a ring that encircles or adorns: hence also the meaning of bordering, festooning, and by extension, that of dominating or adorning.
H3803.emploi: This verb appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in poetry and historical narratives. In Judges 20:43, it describes the military action of surrounding the enemy. In the Psalms (22:13; 142:8), it expresses physical encirclement or close assistance, in contexts of prayer or distress. In Job 36:2, it takes on a nuance of waiting or patient proximity. In Proverbs 14:18, the meaning shifts towards the ornamental or honorific (crown, adornment). In Habakkuk 1:4, it means to surpass or triumph. The context changes the tone: from the concrete to the figurative, from military action to spiritual adornment or victory.
H3803.portee: This word reminds us that we live surrounded — by enemies, by the protection of God, by the righteous who support us. It also invites us to meditate on what "crowns" our life: wisdom is better than folly, and the victory of evil is never final. The image of encirclement urges the believer to seek refuge in God when feeling surrounded, and to discern who or what truly deserves to "encircle" their life.

sens: Ornament worn on the head as a sign of royalty
Insignia of power and sovereign dignity
Symbol of honor and distinction
H3804.detail: 1. The crown is the royal ornament that the king or queen wears on their head. In Esther, it is a precious and visible object, as when one puts "the royal crown on her head" to make a woman queen (Esther 2:17). 2. It represents the power and authority of the sovereign, the sign that someone has authority over a kingdom. Vashti was to wear it to show her royalty and beauty to the peoples (Esther 1:11). 3. It also symbolizes the honor and dignity received: a simple horse can receive "a royal crown" to signify that it is destined for the king (Esther 6:8), thus marking an exceptional honor or distinction.
H3804.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of encircling or surrounding: a crown is that which surrounds and encircles the head. It is the visible insignia of royal power throughout the ancient Near East, and the biblical text mentions it mainly in royal narratives where it marks the transfer of power or the dignity of the one who wears it.
H3804.emploi: The word appears three times in Esther, all related to Persian royalty. It first designates the ornament that the queen must wear to show her beauty and the power of the king (Esther 1:11), then that which is placed on Esther's head to proclaim her queen in place of Vashti (Esther 2:17). Finally, it is mentioned as the insignia of the king, including on the horse intended to honor someone (Esther 6:8). In each case, it marks supreme authority or royal honor.
H3804.portee: The crown reminds the reader that true power belongs to God alone. In the book of Esther, where God is never named, it is precisely through these human ornaments and honors that divine Providence acts, elevating Esther to queen and saving her people. This invites the believer to look beyond royal appearances and recognize that all true power and honor come from God.

sens: Upper part of a column that crowns the shaft
Architectural ornament in the shape of a crown or basket
H3805.detail:
1. The capital is the section that tops the shaft (the body) of a column. It is the element that connects the column to what it supports and serves as a visual and architectural transition. In Solomon's temple, the bronze capitals that crowned the two large columns Jakin and Boaz measured five cubits in height (1 Kings 7:16), making them massive and imposing elements.
2. The capital carries decorations: the text describes how latticework and rows of bronze pomegranates wrapped around these capitals, ornaments that highlighted the richness and splendor of the temple (1 Kings 7:18, 7:20). This decoration reminds us that among the Hebrews, even architectural elements served to express the glory of God in the sanctuary.
H3805.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of what envelops, covers, or crowns. The image is that of a crown placed above, a head or an adorned summit. It is a specifically architectural term used to designate this distinctive part of the column.
H3805.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in descriptions of Solomon's temple and the temple destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar. It mainly appears in the detailed account of the temple's construction (1 Kings 7, 2 Chronicles 4) and in the reports of its destruction (2 Kings 25, Jeremiah 52). In each mention, the capital is described precisely: its dimensions, its decoration (pomegranates, latticework), and its position atop the columns. The use of the term remains consistent: it is always this same ornamental architectural part.
H3805.portee: This word invites the reader to contemplate the beauty and order of God's sanctuary. The capitals adorned with pomegranates symbolize a form of consecrated wealth, where art and material serve to honor the Lord. For the Christian, this architectural detail reminds us that God loves excellence and beauty in the worship rendered to Him.

sens: Reduce to fine powder by striking repeatedly with a tool
Mix substances by crushing them together
Crush, completely grind down
H3806.detail:
1. To pound means to strike something repeatedly with a pestle (a heavy tool) to reduce it to fine powder: this is what is done with grain, spices, or other solid materials in a mortar. In Proverbs 27:22, the image is that of the pestle striking the fool as one would pound grain: the intention is to transform or correct him, but "his folly will not depart from him."
2. To pound can also refer to the action of mixing substances by crushing them together, as one prepares certain foods or remedies by grinding them in a mortar.
3. Figuratively, to pound evokes the idea of completely crushing something, reducing it to nothing: this is why the image in Proverbs 27:22 is so striking — even if one pounds the fool like grain, his folly remains.
H3806.origine: The Hebrew verb kâtash comes from a root that evokes the act of striking, hitting. Its primary meaning is very concrete and tangible: the repeated action of the pestle striking. This image of daily work in the kitchen — pounding, grinding, reducing — has allowed biblical authors to speak figuratively of transformation and crushing.
H3806.emploi: The verb kâtash appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 27:22. This unique usage shows it employed in a highly figurative manner: the fool ("the simpleton," one who refuses wisdom) is compared to grain being pounded. It is a strong image to convey that even the most energetic efforts will not change one who persists in evil. The sapiential (wisdom) context gives the word its full moral and pedagogical significance.
H3806.portee: This verse reminds us of a dark and humble truth: there is no method, even energetic, that can force someone to change if they cling to their folly. The Christian learns from this image that true transformation does not come from our strenuous efforts, but from the conversion of the heart. It is a call not to expend energy correcting one who refuses instruction, but to pray and witness wisely.

sens: Strike or grind something to reduce it to pieces, powder
Shape metal by striking
Defeat, beat someone in battle
Collide, bump into each other
Be broken, destroyed
H3807.detail:
1. It is primarily the act of striking something to destroy or transform it: one reduces to powder what one strikes. Leviticus 22:24 speaks of "crushed" testicles, meaning damaged by blows or pressure.
2. This same act of striking becomes art when shaping metal: Isaiah 2:4 describes how swords will be forged into plowshares, transforming the weapon by hammering.
3. On the battlefield, to crush means to defeat: Deuteronomy 1:44 recounts how the Amorites defeated and crushed them militarily.
4. The word can also simply describe a shock, a collision: 2 Chronicles 15:6 states that people "bumped into" each other, city against city.
5. Finally, to be crushed can mean to be broken, ruined, annihilated: Job 4:20 says that from morning to evening men are "broken" and perish.
H3807.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of striking, hitting. It is linked to the image of the hammer, the violent shock that transforms or destroys. The same root appears in other forms to express various intensities: striking lightly or reducing to crumbs, defeating militarily or simply colliding. It is a very concrete verb, always depicting a physical action.
H3807.emploi: This verb appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, in very varied contexts. Leviticus 22:24 uses it for physical damage. Battle accounts (Deuteronomy 1:44, Jeremiah 46:5) use it to describe a military defeat. Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3 use it poetically to speak of transforming weapons into tools of peace. Job and the Psalms use it figuratively to express ruin or destruction. Two Chronicles 15:6 uses it for a simple shock between peoples. The context changes the meaning: physical (crushed testicles), military (defeated armies), metaphorical (broken by misfortune), or transformative (forged metal).
H3807.portee: This word shows us how the Bible speaks of evil and defeat: not in an abstract way, but in concrete images of shock and destruction. But it also shows us, in Isaiah, that God can transform this act of destruction into a creative act — forging weapons into tools of peace. It is an invitation to see that God's power can turn violence into construction if peoples turn to Him.

sens: Negation of existence, reality, or possession
Refusal or prohibition
Absence or lack of something
Negation of identity or nature
Negation concerning time (never, not yet)
Deprivation or exclusion
H3808.detail:
1. When it is said that something does not exist or is not true: "There was no grass on the earth" (Genesis 2:5). This is the simplest usage, denying a reality.
2. When something is forbidden or one refuses to do it: "You shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil" (Genesis 2:17). The word carries the divine order of refusal.
3. When something is lacking: "There was no man to till the ground" (Genesis 2:5). The absence is total.
4. When one denies that something is of such nature: "The Egyptian is man and not god" (Isaiah 31:3). One affirms a true nature by denying the false.
5. When one denies what will last forever: "There shall never be a flood to destroy the earth" (Genesis 9:11). This is a negation that extends into the future.
6. When one dismisses someone or something: "You shall not violate any right" (Deuteronomy 16:19). This means that there must be no trace of that.
H3808.origine: It is a fundamental negative particle in Hebrew, with a simple and ancient root. It opposes affirmation ("yes, it is") by purely refusing. It is a word that every Hebrew speaker used from childhood. It also exists in Aramaic in the form la (לָא), showing that it is stable in the ancient Semitic languages of the Near East.
H3808.emploi: This word appears more than 3900 times in the Old Testament, making it one of the most frequent words in the Hebrew Bible. It is found everywhere: in divine orders (prohibitions of the Decalogue), in narratives (to say that something did not happen), in dialogues (to deny or refuse), in poetry, and in laws. Its meaning changes in depth according to the context: absolute and terrible when God forbids something ("You shall not eat"), more conversational when Abraham responds to God ("No, Lord"), almost reassuring when affirming that God will not abandon His people. In Genesis 4:7, the negation addresses sin that wants to dominate Cain: it is an exhortation to mastery.
H3808.portee: Understanding this small word is to grasp how the Bible sets its limits and prohibitions. When God says "no," it is never out of cruelty: it is to protect, to clarify, to call to obedience. God's refusal liberates as much as it binds. For today's reader, this word reminds us that a biblical life is not the absence of rules, but the clear awareness of what builds us up and what destroys us.

sens: simple negation: absence or prohibition
negation of fact: nothing, none
emphatic negation: never, rather than
unlimited negation: at discretion, without measure
H3809.detail:
1. This Aramaic word expresses the most basic negation, prohibiting an action or denying a fact. For example: in Ezra 5:5, "the work was allowed to continue" literally translates as "not to stop" — not to cease the action.
2. It can indicate the complete absence of something: "no" hand, "nothing" of defect. In Daniel 2:34 and 2:45, the stone is cut out "without the help of any hand," meaning without human intervention.
3. Sometimes it expresses a resolute opposition or an absolute preference, as in Daniel 3:28: the servants delivered their bodies "rather" than serve another god — they categorically refuse.
4. In the context of unlimited quantity, it means "without restriction": "salt at discretion" (Ezra 7:22) means salt without a set limit, at will.
H3809.origine: This Aramaic word derives from the same root as the Hebrew לֹא (lô, "not"), both stemming from a primitive Semitic root expressing negation. In Aramaic, it carries the same fundamental value: to refuse, to prohibit, to annihilate. The Aramaic passages of the Greek New Testament (such as in Mark 5:39) retain this original Aramaic form.
H3809.emploi: This word appears 60 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the Aramaic portions: Ezra and Daniel (and Jeremiah 10:11). It functions as the exact equivalent of the Hebrew negation in the official texts of the Persian administration in Ezra, and in the narratives and visions of Daniel. It never has variations of tense or mood: it is an adverb or an invariable particle. Its fundamental meaning (simple negation) largely dominates, but depending on the context, it can mark total absence ("none"), resolute prohibition, or absence of limit.
H3809.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that God masters refusal and absence: He can block human powers (Ezra 5:5), and His servants can refuse idolatry without fear (Daniel 3:28). Negation before God is never definitive — it rather marks faithfulness in the face of the powers of the world.

sens: City of Manasseh in Gilead, east of the Jordan
H3810.detail: Lodebar is a city located in Gilead, in the region of Manasseh, east of the Jordan. Its Hebrew name לֹא דְבָר (lo devar) literally means "no pasture" or "without pasture," evoking a barren or less fertile area. The Bible mentions this city primarily as the refuge of Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, before King David discovers him and shows him favor (2 Samuel 9:4-5). It is also mentioned as the place of origin of Makir, son of Ammiel, who was among those who provided for David during his flight from Absalom (2 Samuel 17:27).
H3810.origine: The name Lodebar comes from the Hebrew לֹא דְבָר (lo devar), where לֹא (lo) means "no" or "not" and דְבָר (devar) refers to a "pasture" or "meadow." This descriptive name reflects the geographical nature of the place: a region of Gilead known to be less fertile or devoid of good pastures. The name also appears in the form Lidvir (לִדְבִר) in some ancient texts.
H3810.emploi: Lodebar appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, all occurrences found in the books of Samuel and Amos. It is first identified as the house where Mephibosheth, the disabled son of Jonathan, lived, hidden there under the protection of Makir after the death of Saul (2 Samuel 9:4-5). It reappears as the city of origin of Makir, who provided assistance to David during his flight (2 Samuel 17:27). The prophet Amos also mentions it in his prophetic message (Amos 6:13). Lodebar remains a secondary place in the biblical narrative, but it plays an important role in the story of David's mercy towards the survivors of Saul's house.
H3810.portee: The story of Lodebar teaches the power of grace: Mephibosheth, hidden and forgotten in this remote city, is found by David who not only spares him but shows him unexpected kindness. This account illustrates how God can restore one who seems lost or marginalized. The very name of the city, "without pasture," contrasts with the abundance that David offers to Mephibosheth, an image of divine generosity towards the weak.

sens: To be tired, exhausted from effort or hardship
To be discouraged, impatient, losing courage in the face of difficulty
To find something burdensome, difficult to bear
To tire someone out, wear them down through repeated effort
H3811.detail:
1. The word primarily describes a physical state of exhaustion: to be tired, weary of strength. In Genesis 19:11, the men struck with blindness exert themselves in a "futile effort" to find the door — they tire themselves without result.
2. It also expresses moral discouragement, the loss of energy in the face of adversity. In Job 4:5, the righteous are reproached: "you are weakening" when the trial reaches you — it is to lose courage.
3. The word can mean that something seems burdensome or difficult to accomplish. In Proverbs 26:15, the sluggard finds it "burdensome" to bring his hand to his mouth — even minimal effort tires him.
4. Used in the sense of "causing fatigue," it means to wear out: in Jeremiah 20:9, the prophet "strives" to contain the inner fire that burns within him — he exhausts himself resisting.
H3811.origine: This Hebrew verb expresses the fundamental idea of effort that consumes energy. The root suggests gradual wear, exhaustion. It appears in contexts where pain, difficulty, or impatience dominate. The word belongs to the common language of the Old Testament to describe the human condition in the face of trials and the limits of one's strength.
H3811.emploi: The verb appears about 18 times in the Old Testament. It is frequent among the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah) who denounce human or divine impatience: God says in Isaiah 1:14 that the festivals "weary" Him. It is also found in Proverbs to describe laziness, and in narratives where characters are overwhelmed by trials. The meaning varies: sometimes it is physical fatigue, sometimes moral discouragement, sometimes irritated impatience. In divine speech (Jeremiah 15:6, Micah 6:3), the word expresses God's weariness in the face of His people's unfaithfulness.
H3811.portee: This word reminds us that fatigue — both physical and moral — is a real experience known to God. It should not bring us shame: it is human. But it also warns us not to wear ourselves out through impatience or discouragement, and to listen when the Lord expresses His weariness in the face of our unfaithfulness. It is an invitation to spiritual vigilance and perseverance.

sens: Wife of Jacob during the patriarchal period, mother of six sons and one daughter
Eldest of Laban's two daughters, less loved than her younger sister Rachel
H3812.detail:
1. Leah is a woman from the time of the patriarchs, Jacob's first wife. She becomes the mother of Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Dinah. Her story unfolds mainly in the Book of Genesis, where she shares Jacob's marital life with her sister Rachel.

2. Leah is the eldest of Laban's two daughters; unlike her younger sister Rachel, she is not the one Jacob loves. Although married to Jacob first (through Laban's trickery in Genesis 29:23-25), she remains the less loved one (Genesis 29:30). However, it is she who gives Jacob his first sons, and the Lord sees her maternal distress (Genesis 29:31-32).
H3812.origine: The name literally means "weary" or "tired" in Hebrew. This meaning could evoke her humble role as one who works, less beautiful or less noticed than her sister. Leah lived during the time of the three patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, a foundational period in the history of Israel.
H3812.emploi: Leah appears 34 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in Genesis (chapters 29 to 46) and one mention in Ruth 4:11. The main narratives recount her forced marriage to Jacob (Genesis 29:16-30), her fruitful motherhood despite her husband's lack of love (Genesis 30), her children who will found the tribes of Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah — from whom Judah will be the ancestor of Jesus (Genesis 35:23). She is mentioned as a witness to her family's major decisions, for example when Jacob wants to return to the land of Canaan (Genesis 31:14), and she is buried there (Genesis 49:31; Ruth 4:11 honors her among the mothers of Israel).
H3812.portee: Leah embodies the hidden dignity of one whom the world despises or forgets. Although loved less than her sister and married through deception, she becomes the mother of four of the twelve tribes of Israel, including Judah, from whom the Messiah will come. Her story teaches that God's favor does not always follow human judgment: it is Leah, not Rachel, who gives Israel its most important ancestors. It also shows how God sees and blesses maternal distress and silent faithfulness.

sens: To cover the face with a cloth or garment
To publicly express shame, mourning, or distress
H3813.detail:
1. In the literal sense, it is to cover the face with a cloth, garment, or mantle. David does this to hide in a sign of shame and affliction after the death of Absalom (2 Samuel 19:4).
2. In a figurative and deeper sense, covering one's face means to publicly express great pain, shame, or distress. The gesture is visible, addressing all: King David does not try to hide his grief in private; he manifests it before all with his veiled face, and he cries out his despair.
H3813.origine: The Hebrew verb לאַט (la'at) literally means "to cover." The root evokes the action of draping, veiling. This specific gesture of the face is a well-known sign of mourning and penitence in the ancient Near East: one covers the head and face to manifest an emotion too strong to be contained.
H3813.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 19:4. David, after learning of his son Absalom's death in battle, covers his face as a sign of extreme mourning. This specific context shows that the gesture is not an act of ordinary shame, but the expression of a public royal affliction, where the father openly weeps for the loss of his beloved son.
H3813.portee: This word reminds us that crying and showing one's grief are not signs of weakness: even a king can cover his face in pain. The Bible allows and recognizes deep emotions in the face of loss. It is an invitation not to suppress sadness but to express it authentically before God and others.

sens: magical or supernatural art practiced in secret
action performed discreetly, without noise or haste
H3814.detail:
1. The word first designates a hidden, mysterious art: the enchantments of the Egyptian magicians (Exodus 7:11) who imitate God's wonders. It is a reserved knowledge, often linked to occult or esoteric practices — something not shown in the open, practiced in the shadows.
2. In a more concrete and everyday sense, the word applies to anything done slowly, gently, quietly: when Jael approaches "gently" Sisera, who is asleep, to kill him (Judges 4:21), she acts discreetly, without haste, so as not to wake him. The common idea is one of secrecy, discretion — either mystery and magic, or simple discretion and slowness.
H3814.origine: The Hebrew word lat comes from a root that expresses the idea of what is hidden, reserved, secret. It can refer to a mysterious and veiled action (hence "enchantment") or simply to what is done without haste, gradually (hence "gently"). The basic image is that of secrecy, the non-manifest: what is not seen, what escapes the gaze or the noise.
H3814.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 7:11, it designates the "enchantments" or magical arts of the Egyptian magicians, which rival God's signs — this is the mysterious and occult sense. In Judges 4:21, the same word means "gently," "without noise," to describe how Jael approaches the weapon of the sleeping warrior — this is the sense of discretion and slowness. Both uses share the idea of what is done outside direct sight, either through a hidden art or through a silent action.
H3814.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Bible takes occult practices and magical arts seriously as realities, while showing that true signs come only from God. It also invites reflection on the contrast between what is done in the open and what remains hidden — a distinction that the Christian conscience must learn to discern.

sens: father of Eliasaph, chief of the Gershonites
H3815.detail: Lael is a Levite from the tribe of Levi, ancestor of the Gershonite clan. He is the father of Eliasaph, who was designated as the chief of the paternal house of this group at the time of the census of the Levites in the wilderness (Numbers 3:24).
H3815.origine: The name Lael means "belonging to God" or "God is my," formed from the particle "la" (to, for) and the divine name "El" (God). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing the idea that the person belongs to God or depends on Him.
H3815.emploi: Lael appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 3:24. He is mentioned as the father of Eliasaph during the census of the Levites organized by Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. His name is included in the genealogy of the Gershonite clan, one of the three major families of Levi, responsible for transporting the tabernacle and its elements.

sens: A group of men and women sharing a community of life, language, or destiny under a common authority
A large human group, as opposed to leaders or elites
Population of a territory or nation, considered in its political or military capacity
H3816.detail: 1. A people is primarily a community of united individuals: in Genesis 25:23, the Lord announces to Rebekah that "two peoples will separate from your womb," referring to the descendants of her two sons, Esau and Jacob, who will each form a great nation with its own destiny. 2. The word often emphasizes the people as a mass, distinct from those who govern it: in Proverbs 14:28, "When the people is numerous, it is the glory of a king," we see that the strength and prosperity of a king depend on the greatness of his people. 3. It is also a historical and political reality: in Isaiah 17:13, the nations "roar like the roaring of great waters," an image of powers that can threaten, which God can scatter like the wind scatters chaff. 4. In a religious context, it is the community under God's judgment: in Psalms 9:9, the Lord "judges the peoples with righteousness," which implies that God has authority and responsibility over all human groups.
H3816.origine: The Hebrew word לְאֹם (le'om) properly designates an assembly, a gathering, and comes from a root expressing the idea of coming together or forming a group. It is related to the concept of tribe or community organized around a common ancestor. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), it often translates the Hebrew עַם (am, people) or גוֹי (goy, nation), all three designating a human collective, but le'om emphasizes the aspect of a united assembly more than just a mass.
H3816.emploi: The word appears 27 times in the Old Testament, particularly in Psalms and Isaiah. It is encountered mostly when speaking of several peoples or nations together: the foreign peoples who roar against Israel, the nations that God judges or subdues. In Proverbs, it designates the people in relation to their king or to justice (Proverbs 14:28, 14:34). In Isaiah 43:9 and 49:1, the context is that of God's call to the peoples. The word rarely appears alone to designate Israel: when it does, it is in a context where Israel is seen as a people among the peoples, subjected to God's judgment or grace.
H3816.portee: Meditating on the word "people" invites the Christian to see themselves as a member of a community united by their faith in Christ, not just as an isolated individual. It also shows that God judges nations and peoples according to His justice, and that no human power escapes His authority. For the Church, it is a reminder that we are a people called by God, with a collective vocation and responsibility before Him.

sens: People descended from Dedan, mentioned in the genealogy of the patriarchs
H3817.detail: Leummim is a people whose eponymous ancestor is Dedan, himself the son of Jokshan. This name appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 25:3, where it is listed among the descendants of Jokshan along with the Ashurim and the Letushim. Like the other peoples from this genealogical branch, the Leummim are presented as tribes or peoples of the ancient Near East, likely nomadic or semi-nomadic, but no other biblical detail describes them.
H3817.origine: The name Leummim literally means "peoples" or "nations." It is a collective name formed from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of human grouping. It is a typical eponymous name from Genesis: the name of the people derives from that of its presumed founding ancestor.
H3817.emploi: Leummim appears only once in the entire Bible, in Genesis 25:3. This genealogy of the sons of Abraham classifies Leummim among the descendants of Abraham through Keturah (his concubine after the death of Sarah), and more specifically as one of the three peoples descended from Dedan. The biblical text provides no further information about this people: neither its precise geographical location, nor its customs, nor its relations with other peoples of Israel.

sens: Son of the prophet Hosea and Gomer
Symbolic name meaning "not my people"
Sign of the rupture of the covenant between God and Israel
H3818.detail:
1. Lo-Ammi is the second son that the prophet Hosea had with Gomer. He appears only once in the Bible, in Hosea 1:9, where the Lord commands the prophet to give him this particular name.

2. This name literally means "not my people" in Hebrew. It is a symbolic name, not a mere nickname: it expresses a prophetic message. Hosea 1:9 explains its meaning: "Give him the name Lo-Ammi; for you are not my people, and I am not your God."

3. This name represents God's judgment on Israel because of its unfaithfulness. By giving this name to his son, Hosea acts as a living prophet: his family becomes a sign, a warning. The people that God once called "my people" has turned away through idolatry and sin, so that God must say: you are no longer my people.
H3818.origine: The name Lo-Ammi comes from Hebrew: "lo" means "not, no" and "ammi" means "my people." It is a very direct construction, a refusal expressed in two words. This name contrasts with another prophetic name that Hosea gives to his first son: Jezreel, which evokes divine judgment, and with that of his daughter: Lo-Ruhamah, which means "not loved." Together, these three names form a prophetic message of abandonment and rupture. Note that this name implicitly responds to another name of Israel: "Ammi," meaning "my people," which God used for His covenant with Jacob (Exodus 19:5-6). By giving the name Lo-Ammi, God removes this title of honor.
H3818.emploi: Lo-Ammi appears only once in the Bible, in Hosea 1:9. However, this unique usage is loaded with prophetic meaning. The prophet Hosea was commanded to give symbolic names to his three children with Gomer to signify the state of Northern Israel at this time of spiritual decline. The name Lo-Ammi, given to the second son, precisely expresses the rupture of the covenant: the chosen people of God, once called by the loving name "my people," is now denied this title because of its unfaithfulness. It is a severe judgment, but it also carries a hidden promise: in Hosea 2:1, God says that the children of Israel will be called "Ammi" and "Ruhamah" — meaning that this rupture will not be eternal.
H3818.portee: The name Lo-Ammi reminds the believer that the relationship with God is based on covenant and faithfulness. Being called "the people of God" is not a title acquired once and for all, but a gift to be preserved through obedience. This dark name, however, carries a hope: it announces a temporary judgment, not a definitive one. For the Christian, this sheds light on the seriousness of our commitment to God and the grace that restores us when we stray from Him.

sens: Daughter of the prophet Hosea and Gomer
Symbolic name meaning 'No Mercy' or 'Without Compassion'
H3819.detail:
1. Lo-Ruchama is the daughter that the prophet Hosea had with Gomer. She is mentioned for the first time in Hosea 1:6, where the Lord commands the prophet to give her this particular name. She had an older brother named Jezreel and a younger brother named Lo-Ammi ('Not-My-People').

2. This name is not just a nickname: it is a prophetic message. The Lord explains to Hosea why he must call his daughter this: 'for I will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel' (Hosea 1:6). The name literally means 'No Mercy' or 'Without Compassion.' Every time the parents called their daughter, they reminded Israel that after so many transgressions, God would temporarily turn away from His people and withdraw His mercy.
H3819.origine: The Hebrew name לֹא רֻחָמָה (lo rouhamah) is composed of לֹא (lo, 'no') and רַחַם (ra'ham, 'to have mercy, show compassion'). The root רחם literally evokes the womb, hence the idea of maternal tenderness and compassion. By denying this compassion with the particle לֹא, the name expresses the temporary withdrawal of divine grace. It is a theophoric name, carrying a sacred meaning, typical of Hosea's prophecy where each child embodies a message.
H3819.emploi: Lo-Ruchama appears only twice in the Bible, both in Hosea 1. The first mention (Hosea 1:6) reports the divine command to give this name to the newborn daughter and explains its meaning: it is a sign of the impending judgment on the house of Israel. The second mention (Hosea 1:8) is brief: it notes that Lo-Ruchama was weaned, marking the passage of time in the prophet's family life. These two verses constitute all that the Bible tells us about this child; her very existence was a prophetic act meant to convince Israel of the reality of God's anger.
H3819.portee: The life of Lo-Ruchama teaches Christians that God's mercy, while certain in the long term, can be temporarily suspended due to persistent sin. It is an invitation to repentance, not despair: the name 'No Mercy' is not eternal. Later, Hosea 2:3 announces that God will transform this name into a blessing ('You have found mercy'), showing that even judgment is educational and open to restoration.

sens: The physical organ at the center of the body, seat of life
What one thinks, knows, understands
What one wants, decides to do
What one desires, loves, fears
The moral character of a person, their integrity or corruption
Courage, firmness, self-confidence
H3820A.detail:
1. The heart is primarily the central physical organ of the body. In Exodus 15:8, Pharaoh's heart becomes hardened like stone in the face of the plagues of Egypt: the physical image of hardening expresses the stubborn refusal to obey.

2. The heart is the seat of thought and knowledge. In Ecclesiastes 1:13, the one who applies their heart to seek means that they reflect, that they understand through study. It is where conscious thoughts and knowledge are born.

3. The heart is the place of decisions and will. In Genesis 27:41, Esau keeps in his heart the intention to kill Jacob: he firmly nurtures this resolution. It is the will that sets and acts.

4. The heart is the seat of desires, emotions, and passions. In Genesis 34:3, Shechem loves Dinah and his heart is attached to her: the heart is where feelings are born and grow. In 2 Samuel 13:28, the heart gladdened by wine expresses fleeting joy.

5. The heart reveals a person's moral character. In Genesis 6:5, the thoughts of men's hearts are only inclined toward evil: it is in the heart that inner corruption is revealed. In Proverbs 2:10, wisdom enters and dwells there.

6. The heart can be strong or weak, courageous or fearful. In Deuteronomy 28:65, God gives the people a trembling heart, an oppressive anxiety: the weak heart is incapable of trust.
H3820A.origine: The Hebrew word לֵב (lev) comes from a very ancient root meaning the center, the interior. As in many languages, the physical heart becomes the image of all that is internal and hidden: thoughts, feelings, will, conscience. This same root has given rise to other words associated with the inside, the center, the secret. In the Greek Septuagint, the word lev is regularly translated as καρδία (kardia), which carries exactly the same range of meanings from the physical to the moral and spiritual.
H3820A.emploi: The word לֵב (heart) is one of the most frequent words in the Hebrew Bible (about 550 occurrences). It appears mainly in historical narratives (Genesis, Exodus, Samuel), in the Psalms, and in Proverbs. Its use varies according to the context: in Pharaoh, the hardened heart stubbornly refuses the word of God (Exodus 7:13, 9:12, 10:1); among the faithful people, the generous heart freely offers for the offerings to the tabernacle (Exodus 25:2, 35:5); in wisdom, the heart becomes the seat of intelligence and reflection (Proverbs 2:10, Ecclesiastes 1:13). The heart can be joyful, sad, hard, broken, filled with hatred or love: it is always the personal center from which the conduct of the entire being emanates.
H3820A.portee: The heart according to the Bible is not primarily a feeling, but the center of the person from which thoughts, decisions, and actions spring forth. Understanding this transforms the reading of faith: God does not look at outward appearances; He examines the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). This calls the believer to seek inner sincerity, an obedience that comes from within. Pharaoh's hardened heart and the generous heart of the faithful show that our heart does not belong to us: it is where God works to transform who we truly are.

sens: The part of the body where emotions and feelings reside
The seat of thought, will, and desires
The intimate and deep part of a person
The vital center, what is essential
H3820B.detail:
1. The heart is primarily the physical organ, but in the Bible, it signifies much more: the seat of emotions. When one is afraid, one has 'a racing heart'; when one is joyful, 'the heart exults.'
2. The heart is also the place of thought and moral conscience. It is where intentions, plans, and deep desires form. God 'searches the hearts' because He sees what no one else sees: our true motivations.
3. By extension, the heart designates the intimate being of a person, their integrity or faithfulness. A 'whole' or 'perfect' heart before God means complete sincerity, without hypocrisy.
4. The heart can also mean the center or core of something — the essence, what makes it alive. Thus 'the heart of the sea' is the middle of the sea, 'the heart of the day' is the hottest moment.
H3820B.origine: The Hebrew word לֵב (lev) is a very ancient term, common to all Semitic languages. It literally designates the organ of the heart, but from the earliest origins, it has taken on a figurative meaning to evoke all that is hidden deep within: feelings, thoughts, will. This richness of the word reflects the biblical vision: the heart is not just a muscle; it is the true seat of the person, well before intellect alone.
H3820B.emploi: The word לֵב (lev) appears hundreds of times in the Old Testament, across all literary genres: history, poetry, prophecy. It constantly designates the center of a person's or a people's emotional, moral, and spiritual life. Among the prophets, one often finds the call to 'return one's heart to God' or the reproach of a hardened heart, turned away. The context can clarify it: 'wise heart,' 'proud heart,' 'contrite heart'; or the action: 'seek with all your heart,' 'love with all your heart.' God Himself is said to have a heart, thus describing His feelings or will.
H3820B.portee: Understanding that the Bible speaks of the heart is to grasp that it never isolates reason or will: it always aims at the whole person, with their emotions, inner convictions, and authenticity. For the believer, this means that God is not satisfied with external or correct acts: He seeks a sincere, transformed heart that truly desires Him. It is an invitation to honesty towards oneself and towards God.

sens: The physical organ that animates the body
The seat of feelings and emotions
The inner self of a person, what they think and deeply desire
Attention, mental concentration
H3821.detail: 1. The heart is primarily the organ of the body that gives life, as in modern French. However, the Bible refers to it well beyond this biological reality. 2. It is the seat of feelings: joy, fear, and sadness take root there. In the Aramaic of the book of Daniel, when Daniel is troubled by his thoughts (Daniel 7:28), it is his heart that receives and retains what moves him. 3. Even more profoundly, the heart is the inner being of a human — their true thoughts, hidden desires, what motivates them at their core. When one "keeps something in their heart," they do not forget it; they return to it constantly. 4. Finally, the heart also denotes the concentration of the mind, the will directed toward something: one who listens with all their heart brings their full attention to it.
H3821.origine: This Aramaic word exactly corresponds to the Hebrew word לֵב (lev) from the Old Testament. Both derive from a very ancient root that primarily expresses the idea of the center, of what is in the middle of something. The heart, physically in the middle of the body, thus becomes the perfect image of the center of a person, where their true nature resides.
H3821.emploi: This word appears only once in the provided verses, in chapter 7 of the book of Daniel, which is written in Aramaic (not in Hebrew like the rest of the Old Testament). Daniel reports that he kept the terrifying visions he received in his heart. It is a key word throughout the Bible to denote the seat of inner life — thoughts, emotions, intentions, faith. The Aramaic of Daniel uses this exact term to show that even the secrets of the prophet's soul remain engraved deep within his being.
H3821.portee: The heart, in biblical language, is never simply the organ of a machine. It is the place where God seeks our true attachment, where our true decisions are forged, where our faith germinates. When Daniel keeps these words in his heart, he does not forget them; he meditates on them, allowing them to transform his inner self. This word reminds us that faith is not just a matter of intellect: it engages all that we are, at the deepest level.

sens: City in the south of Judah
H3822.detail: Lebaoth is a small city in the south of Judah, listed among the cities of the tribe. It appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:32, in the list of localities assigned to Judah after the conquest of Canaan.
H3822.origine: The name means "witness" (in Hebrew, from the root indicating testimony). This meaning reflects the importance that the ancient Israelites attached to place names, often linked to events or characteristics of the site.
H3822.emploi: Lebaoth is mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in Joshua 15:32, as one of the thirty-nine cities in the lot of Judah. Its name appears in a geographical enumeration without a specific narrative attached to its history.

sens: To capture, seduce someone's affection
To awaken intelligence, make someone wise
H3823A.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of capturing the heart, deeply seducing someone. In Song of Solomon 4:9, the lover says, "You have captivated my heart": it is the image of a heart literally stolen, carried away by the beauty and love of the other. The word evokes an irresistible and passionate attraction.
2. In a more sober sense, the word can mean "to make someone wise, to give them understanding." In Job 11:12, "Man is born like a wild donkey" uses this word to speak of the ability to understand and have common sense. It is less about seduction than about the illumination of the mind.
H3823A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that literally means "heart." In Hebrew, the heart is not just the physical organ: it is the center of emotions, will, and intelligence. The verb "to captivate the heart" thus images the action of seizing, capturing this vital center. The form of the verb used (Piel) intensifies the action: it creates the idea of repeated seduction, of continuous enchantment.
H3823A.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Song of Solomon 4:9, it expresses romantic seduction: the lover confesses that his beloved captivates him with a simple glance or by a necklace. In Job 11:12, it describes how a man can acquire wisdom and discernment. Both uses share the idea of an inner transformation: one is either seized by love or illuminated by understanding. The romantic context of the Song shows the emotional power of the word.
H3823A.portee: This word reminds us that the heart is the seat of our affections and our wisdom. In the eyes of the Bible, we do not love only with reason, and we do not acquire wisdom solely through study: the heart is the true center of it. For the Christian, this invites us to guard our hearts diligently (Proverbs 4:23), for it is there that faith, love for God, and spiritual discernment are born.

sens: To shape and bake dough to make flatbreads or cakes
H3823B.detail: 1. The verb describes the action of preparing and baking bread or cakes. In 2 Samuel 13:6, Amnon asks his sister Tamar to come "make cakes" in front of him, which means to shape and bake them before him. The word evokes the concrete work in the kitchen: taking the dough, kneading it, putting it in the fire to bake.
H3823B.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that designates the action of cooking or baking. It belongs to the family of culinary action verbs, which are common in the daily life of Israel. The form used in these instances (Piel) emphasizes the complete accomplishment of the action: not only shaping but truly baking it through.
H3823B.emploi: The word appears twice in the Old Testament, both in the same episode of 2 Samuel 13, where Tamar prepares cakes for her brother Amnon. In 2 Samuel 13:6, it is Amnon who asks Tamar to "make" the cakes; in 2 Samuel 13:8, Tamar goes to her house and "prepares" the cakes before baking them in front of him. In both verses, the word denotes the concrete and complete culinary action: shaping the dough and baking it. It is a mundane action of domestic life, but in this context, it becomes the occasion for a drama.
H3823B.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible speaks of the ordinary gestures of daily life — here the work of cooking — with as much seriousness as great events. It also shows us how the simple details of the narrative (preparing cakes) can serve the hidden intentions of a person and lead to evil. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize that God sees and judges even actions that seem trivial, and that faith begins in our most ordinary gestures.

sens: The physical and spiritual center of a person, the seat of life
Moral conscience and deep intention
Intellect, reason, and memory
Will, resolution, and determination
The seat of emotions and passions
The source of courage or fear
H3824.detail:
1. The heart is the center of the entire human being, what makes one live and act. It is the organ of inner life, where all movements of the soul reside. When Genesis 20:5 says that Abimelech "acted with a pure heart," it means that deep down, his intention was honest.
2. The heart is the place of conscience: it is where one knows if they have acted well or poorly. In 1 Kings 2:44, King David tells Shimei: "You know in your heart all the evil you have done" — what one intimately knows about their own actions is known in their heart.
3. The heart is the instrument of thought, reflection, and memory. It is through the heart that one understands, remembers, and learns. Deuteronomy 4:9 commands to keep the divine Word "carefully in your heart," meaning to meditate on it and retain it through the understanding of the heart.
4. The heart is the seat of will and resolution. To love God "with all your heart" (Deuteronomy 6:5) means to engage one's entire will in that love, to decide to dedicate all one's intention to God.
5. The heart is the source of emotions, desires, and passions — joy, sadness, covetousness, hatred. Isaiah 19:1 speaks of the "heart of the Egyptians" that "fails," meaning it is filled with fear and despair.
6. The heart can also be the seat of courage: Deuteronomy 20:8 speaks of one "whose heart is timid," while Joshua 14:7 asserts that Joshua followed the Lord "with all his heart," showing courageous determination.
H3824.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that designates the central organ of the body. Hebrew does not isolate the heart as a mere pump: it makes it the symbol of all inner life — thought, will, conscience, emotions. It is a fundamental word that occupies biblical thought: the heart is not just a visceral organ; it is equivalent to what we call the soul, spirit, or conscience. Biblical life is a life of the heart because it touches the entirety of the person, not just a particular domain.
H3824.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament, used about 230 times. It spans all books, from narratives to laws, from psalms to prophets. The heart is constant: it is both the seat of moral knowledge (one knows "in their heart" what they have done), the principle of obedient choice ("to love God with all your heart"), and the refuge of human feelings (fear, joy, failure). In Deuteronomy, the exhortation to keep the divine Word "in your heart" and to "observe with all your heart" recurs; in the historical books, we discover men whose hearts are "whole" toward God (1 Kings 8:18: David's plan) or "turned" toward idolatry; in the psalms and prophets, the heart should be purified and humbled. The word reveals how the Bible conceives of obedience: it is not external; it is a matter of the heart.
H3824.portee: The heart taught by the Bible is not the seat of sentimentalities: it is the place where conscience, intelligence, and will converge. The Bible invites us to a whole-hearted commitment to God, which involves truly knowing Him (with our intellect), truly wanting Him (with our will), and feeling this commitment (with our directed emotions). For the Christian, placing "all one's heart" under the lordship of Christ is not a momentary experience but a state of being that engages the whole self.

sens: The physical organ that beats in the chest
The seat of thoughts, intelligence, and reflection
The seat of feelings and emotions
The center of will and decisions
The moral character of a person, their inner disposition
The seat of conscience and reason
H3825.detail:
1. The heart primarily designates the physical organ, as in Daniel 4:16 where God changes the "heart of man" of Nebuchadnezzar into a "heart of beast": the animal neither thinks nor reasons like a man.
2. The heart is the seat of thought and intelligence: in Daniel 2:30, Daniel explains that there is no superior wisdom in him, but the secret has been revealed "so that you may know the thoughts of your heart" — that is, your intimate reflections, your hidden intentions.
3. It is also the heart that experiences feelings: it can rise in pride (Daniel 5:20), become like that of beasts when conscience is extinguished (Daniel 5:21).
4. The heart is the center of moral will: in Daniel 5:22, Belshazzar is blamed for not having "humbled your heart," meaning he did not submit his will and pride to the reality of God.
5. It expresses the inner character of a person: a human heart reflects reason and conscience, a beast's heart the absence of judgment.
H3825.origine: This Aramaic word (לְבַב, lebav) is directly related to the Hebrew לֵבָב (levav, H3824), which also means "heart." It comes from a root that evokes the heart as the vital center of the body and personal life. Hebrew and Aramaic share this same imagery: the heart, this beating organ at the center of the body, becomes the symbol of all that is at the center of a person — their thought, judgment, morality, will. This imagery is common to all ancient Near Eastern languages.
H3825.emploi: The word lebav appears 6 times in Aramaic in the book of Daniel, always referring to the hearts of important characters: Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, a prophetic lion. In all instances, it designates either the seat of thoughts (Daniel 2:30) or the organ whose transformation symbolizes the change of judgment and reason (Daniel 4:16, 5:21, 7:4). The expression "to change the heart" means to take away human wisdom. Several passages (Daniel 5:20, 5:22) associate the heart with pride or humility, showing that it is the seat of moral disposition. The context of Daniel's visions shows that the heart is what makes a person aware of God or, conversely, what distances them from Him through pride.
H3825.portee: Understanding that the heart in the Bible is not primarily emotion, but the center of the person — their thought, conscience, will — helps grasp the seriousness of biblical calls to "give our heart" or to "keep the heart." It is through the heart that a person reasons, judges, decides right from wrong, and recognizes or rejects God. The narratives of Daniel show that the pride of the heart separates from God and that only the humility of the heart allows one to recognize Him. For the Christian, this means that transformation begins at the center of oneself, in this seat of conscience and will.

sens: The physical organ that beats in the chest
The seat of thoughts, feelings, and intentions
The moral conscience, what is deepest within oneself
What deserves approval or blame before God
H3826.detail:
1. The heart is primarily the organ of the human body, the vital center. But in the Hebrew Bible, it means much more: it is the center of all that one is.
2. The heart is the place where thoughts, desires, and feelings originate. It is where a person's true will and intention reside. In Proverbs 21:2, "he who weighs the hearts" sees beyond appearances: he knows the true intentions hidden behind actions.
3. The heart is also the inner moral conscience, distinguishing the righteous from the wicked. In Psalms 7:10, God "tests the hearts and minds": he examines the heart to see if it is upright and sincere, as in Psalms 125:4 where "those whose hearts are pure" receive divine blessings.
4. The heart becomes the place of divine judgment: in Proverbs 17:3, "he who tests hearts is the Lord." God weighs, tests, judges what we truly are at our core, for he sees all that escapes human eyes.
H3826.origine: The Hebrew word לִבָּה (libah) comes from the root לב (leb), which designates the physical heart but also the seat of conscience. In Hebrew as in French, the heart is never just an organ: it is the symbol of the center of the person, the point where body, soul, and spirit meet. The word is used in the Masoretic text and reflects a holistic view of the human being, where the heart is truly the heart of everything.
H3826.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the provided usages, primarily in Psalms and Proverbs, two books that deepen the understanding of oneself and the relationship with God. It constantly returns in the context of divine judgment: God "tests" the hearts (Psalms 7:10), he "examines" them (Proverbs 17:3), and "weighs" them (Proverbs 21:2). The heart is therefore the object of divine scrutiny; it is where God looks to know the truth. The references also show that "the pure heart" (Psalms 125:4) is the moral ideal to strive for, while the wickedness of the heart is what must be avoided.
H3826.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that God does not judge by appearances: he sees the heart. Therefore, one cannot deceive God by presenting a beautiful outward conduct if the heart is not sincere. This invites honesty before God and oneself, to cultivate a pure heart rather than play a role. It is a call to spiritual depth and inner transformation, not mere outward conformity.

sens: Tongue of fire that rises and burns
Sharp point of a weapon (spear tip)
H3827.detail:
1. The flame is the visible tongue of fire that rises and consumes. It is the most concrete image of the word: the fire that burns and emits light. In the burning bush (Exodus 3:2), Moses sees a flame of fire that envelops the bush without destroying it — it is the very sign of divine and miraculous presence.
2. By extension, the word also designates the sharp point of a weapon, such as the blade or tip of a spear. The image comes from the resemblance between a flame that leaps and the pointed tip of a weapon that cuts.
H3827.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that first evokes the idea of something that leaps up, something that rises. The image of the flame — the tongue of fire that ascends — is its primary meaning. The same word can also designate anything that has this sharp and pointed form: the blade of a sword or the tip of a spear share with the flame this quality of leaping sharply upward or forward.
H3827.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in Exodus 3:2, at the moment of the burning bush. The scene is pivotal: Moses is about to receive his call from God. The flame here is not destructive, but revealing — it manifests the presence of the Lord in a miraculous act. The word, although rare in the preserved Old Testament, may also have referred to weapon tips in older or parallel contexts.
H3827.portee: The burning bush that is ablaze without being consumed is one of the strongest images of divine presence in the Old Testament. This flame reveals to Moses that he is on holy ground and that he will be sent to deliver Israel. For the reader, it symbolizes both the holiness of God (who consumes) and his mercy (who preserves): a flame that judges but does not destroy the one who obeys it.

sens: Fragrant white resin burned as perfume
Pure incense composed according to the holy formula
Offering or precious gift
H3828.detail:
1. Incense is a white, fragrant resin that is burned to produce a fragrant smoke. In Exodus 30:34, the Lord commands Moses to prepare a mixture of spices including pure incense in equal parts with other substances. This smoke that rises, as seen in Song of Solomon 3:6 with its "columns of smoke," creates an atmosphere of holiness and beauty.
2. In Israel's worship, incense is not offered haphazardly: it must be prepared according to a precise and holy formula. In Leviticus 2:15 and 6:8, it is "poured" or "added" to grain offerings. It is a mandatory part of the ritual, a detail that shows how every element of worship is regulated by God himself.
3. Due to its price and rarity, incense becomes a symbol of what is precious and valuable. In Isaiah 60:6, the nations bring incense as a worthy gift for the Lord. That is why, in Isaiah 43:23, God says to his people: "You have not offered me […] incense," reproaching the people for not bringing him what is most excellent.
H3828.origine: The Hebrew word לְבֹנָה (lebonah) comes from a root that evokes whiteness (the resin of incense is white) or purification. In Hebrew, this connection to clarity and purity is found. It is an imported substance, probably from southern Arabia, which explains its association with wealth and prestige. It was highly valued throughout the ancient Near East for religious worship and for prestigious uses.
H3828.emploi: Incense appears 21 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Law books (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers) and in the accounts of the Temple (Chronicles, Nehemiah). Its use in the law reveals that it is a constitutive element of daily worship: it accompanies grain offerings, it burns on the altar of incense, it is stored in the Temple. In prophetic passages (Isaiah, Jeremiah), incense becomes the criterion of true worship: God reproaches his people for offering him incense without sincerity of heart, or refuses the incense offered to idols. That is why Jeremiah 6:20 says: "What use is that to me, incense that comes from Sheba?" — God wants the heart, not mere ritual.
H3828.portee: Incense in the Bible reminds the believer that authentic worship combines external beauty (the rising perfume) with inner justice (a pure heart). It is an invitation to offer God not only gestures and words, but the best of oneself. The rising perfume also symbolizes a prayer that ascends to God: it must be sincere and precious in his sight.

sens: City of Ephraim, in Canaan
H3829.detail: Lebona is a small town located in the Promised Land, in the region of Ephraim (the central region of Canaan). It is situated about 5 km west-northwest of Shiloh, an important city of worship for the Lord. The only verse where Lebona is mentioned uses it as a geographical landmark to locate Shiloh in relation to the roads and other places. In Judges 21:19, during the annual feast at Shiloh, Lebona serves as a landmark south of Shiloh to guide the Benjamites who were seeking to abduct young women.
H3829.origine: The Hebrew word לְבוֹנָה (lebonah) literally means "frankincense" (from white incense or olibanum). The city bears this name probably because incense was produced or traded there, or because the name evokes the purity and whiteness associated with the incense used in the worship of the God of Israel.
H3829.emploi: Lebona appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 21:19. It is mentioned as a topographical landmark in a serious historical context: after the other tribes of Israel decided to punish the tribe of Benjamin for a heinous crime, they allowed the surviving young Benjamites to abduct young women during the annual feast of the Lord at Shiloh. Thus, Lebona, located south of Shiloh, marks the boundary of this sacred region.

sens: Garment, piece of fabric worn on the body
Covering, layer that covers something
Figuratively: that which envelops, characterizes, or in which one wraps oneself spiritually
H3830.detail:
1. The garment is primarily a concrete item, a piece of fabric that one wears for covering and protection. In Genesis 49:11, the garment is stained with wine, an image of wealth and abundance. In Job 24:7, the poor have no clothing and shiver with cold: it is the covering that is lacking for the naked body. In Esther 6:8-10, royal garments signify rank and honor.
2. The garment can also mean a covering or visible layer that envelops: Job 38:14 compares the transformation of the earth to a garment that is put on, and Job 38:9 speaks of clouds that cover like a garment.
3. Figuratively, the garment becomes that which envelops the soul or being: Proverbs 31:25 says that the virtuous woman is clothed with strength and dignity — not with material garments, but with moral and spiritual qualities that characterize and adorn her.
H3830.origine: The Hebrew word לְבוּשׁ (levoush) comes from the root לבש (labash), which means "to clothe, to dress." This root evokes the action of covering oneself, putting something on. The Aramaic word הוא לְבוּשׁ, identical, shows the stability of the concept in both Semitic languages. The basic image is that of an envelope, that which covers and protects.
H3830.emploi: The word appears 33 times in the Old Testament, especially in the books of wisdom and poetry (Job, Psalms, Proverbs), as well as in historical narratives (Esther, 2 Samuel, 2 Kings). Often, it designates clothing as a material and everyday reality: mourning garment (sackcloth in Psalms 69:12), royal or honorable clothing (Esther 6:8-11), clothing that is torn as a sign of grief. But the Bible also broadens its usage: it uses the word to speak of that which covers (clouds, divine glory), and figuratively to express that which characterizes or adorns a person (strength, dignity in Proverbs 31:25, or feelings in Psalms 35:13 where the psalmist puts on humiliation). This progression from the concrete to the spiritual shows how the Bible enriches material language to speak of the inner world.
H3830.portee: This word invites the reader to see in clothing more than just a simple covering of the body: it is a symbol of what identifies, protects, and characterizes us in the eyes of others. For the believer, it reminds us that the weakness of the poor without clothing and the splendor of the king dressed in purple depend not solely on us, but on divine providence. In a spiritual sense, it opens the question: what do we clothe ourselves with? The woman of Proverbs 31 is clothed with strength and dignity: it is an invitation to seek an inner garment, an adornment of the soul rather than an adornment of the body.

sens: that which one wears on the body for covering
set of fabric pieces covering a person
appearance or external aspect of a celestial figure
H3831.detail: 1. The garment is the clothing, that which one puts on to cover the body. In Daniel 3:21, the three young men are bound with their garments — trousers, tunics, coats — before being thrown into the furnace: it is the set of fabric pieces that covers them. 2. The word also designates the general appearance of a person's clothing. In Daniel 7:9, the garment of the Ancient of Days is white like snow: it is the brilliance and purity that envelops him, expressing his heavenly nature and glory. The outer adornment here reveals the holiness and majesty of a divine figure.
H3831.origine: This Aramaic word (le.vush) corresponds in Hebrew to the verb lvsh, which means "to clothe, to dress." The root evokes the action of covering or enveloping the body. The word belongs to the vocabulary of clothing and textiles, from the most practical to the most symbolic.
H3831.emploi: The Aramaic word le.vush appears twice in Daniel, in chapters 3 and 7. In Daniel 3:21, it describes the ordinary clothes of the three young Hebrews — trousers, tunics, coats — which remain on them in the furnace. In Daniel 7:9, it qualifies the white garment of the Ancient of Days in the vision of the heavenly throne. In this second usage, the garment becomes a symbol of purity and divine majesty, revealing through its external appearance the nature and glory of the one who wears it.
H3831.portee: The garment reminds us that our body is to be preserved, but also that our appearance reflects something internal. In Daniel 3, the garments of the three young men do not protect them from the furnace — only faith makes the difference. In Daniel 7, the white garment expresses God's absolute holiness and transcendent justice.

sens: To rush towards ruin or destruction
To go of one's own accord towards inevitable misfortune
To act foolishly while ignoring the consequences
H3832.detail:
1. The word evokes a race, a rapid movement towards something — but what one is rushing towards is loss, ruin, destruction. It is as if one is voluntarily throwing oneself into the abyss. The image is that of a man who, instead of stopping in time, plunges into evil (Proverbs 10:8).
2. More generally, it is to act foolishly while ignoring where it leads. The person "rushes to their ruin" because they refuse wisdom, despise warning, or yield to their passions. This applies to one who speaks lightly (Proverbs 10:10), as well as to one who is led astray by sin (Hosea 4:14).
3. This is not a punishment imposed by God from the outside: it is a path that the fool chooses for themselves. Ruin is the natural and inevitable consequence of their actions, as if wisdom were a harbor and folly a precipice that one sees from afar.
H3832.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that literally means "to throw," "to overturn," "to precipitate." The basic meaning is very concrete: to throw something down, to violently cast it aside. In the passive form (Niphal), it designates one who is thrown down, overturned, crushed. The meaning has extended to the idea of moral or material ruin: to be cast down in one's condition, in one's status, in one's entire life.
H3832.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the Bible, all in the books of wisdom (Proverbs and Hosea). In Proverbs 10:8 and 10:10, it characterizes the fool who, through their light words or mocking winks, "rushes to their ruin" — their folly destroys them. In Hosea 4:14, it is the entire people that rushes to its ruin by prostituting itself and sacrificing to idols instead of following God. The word always emphasizes the idea that destruction comes from oneself: one chooses it through foolish behavior. It is a warning addressed to fools and idolaters.
H3832.portee: This word reminds the reader that there is no middle ground: either one listens to the wisdom of God, or one rushes headlong towards their own ruin. Illness, poverty, condemnation do not fall from the sky; they are the natural fruit of our choices. It is a call to vigilance and the fear of God: to guard one's words, one's gaze, one's heart, is to stay away from the precipice.

sens: Female of the lion
Image of strength, power, and ferocity
Symbol of danger or threat
H3833A.detail:
1. The lioness is the female of the lion, a fierce and wild animal. She is characterized by her remarkable strength and hunting instinct. The psalmist refers to her to evoke formidable enemies that threaten him (Psalms 57:5).

2. The lioness in the Bible evokes the image of raw power, ferocity, and aggression. The prophet Nahum depicts her tearing apart prey, strangling her young, and filling her lairs with carcasses (Nahum 2:13), reinforcing the idea of an indomitable and threatening force.

3. Figuratively, the lioness symbolizes danger, the enemy that attacks mercilessly. In contexts of distress or threat, she represents the adversaries or hostile powers that the believer confronts.
H3833A.origine: The Hebrew word derives from the root meaning "to be strong" or "to be courageous." The lioness naturally embodies this raw strength and power in the animal kingdom. It is an animal well-known in the ancient Near East for its danger and role as a predator.
