Although it is small, it carries significant emotional weight, as it opens a window into the hidden thoughts and regrets of biblical characters: it shows what could have been or what one would like to be.
H3863.emploi: This particle appears 21 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives (Genesis, Samuel) and poetic discourses (Job, Psalms). It has two main uses: to introduce a hypothetical condition, often negative or regretted, as when Balaam says, "If I had a sword" (Numbers 22:29); or to express an intense and unattainable wish, like Abraham exclaiming, "Oh! that Ishmael might live!" (Genesis 17:18). The prophets use it to express God's regret over Israel's unfaithfulness: "If only you had listened to me!" (Isaiah 48:18). It is a particle of intimate discourse, revealing unspoken thoughts and secret desires.
H3863.portee: This particle invites us to recognize regrets, hidden desires, and untraveled paths that dwell in the hearts of men. It reminds us that our human condition is marked by lack and doubt, and that there is always a gap between what is and what we would have liked to be. It also teaches us to listen to the deepest thoughts of those around us, as this particle lays bare the heart. For the believer, it reminds us of the reality of sin and repentance: we live in a world where things could have been different, but where God reigns nonetheless.

sens: inhabitant of Libya, a region of North Africa west of Egypt
H3864.detail: 1. The Libyans are a people from North Africa, living west of Egypt. In the Bible, they appear as neighboring peoples, often allies or vassals of the Egyptians, forming significant armies with them.
H3864.origine: The Hebrew word לוּב (Loub) designates the inhabitants of the region called Libya. This name refers to the populations of northwest Africa, known in antiquity as formidable warriors and horsemen. The word has a straightforward geographical origin: it names the inhabitants according to their land of origin.
H3864.emploi: The word "Libyan" appears only 4 times in the Bible, always in the plural. It is found in historical narratives involving Egypt and its military allies: during Shishak's invasion of Judah (2 Chronicles 12:3), in the military context of the Ethiopians and Libyans under King Asa (2 Chronicles 16:8), in Daniel's prophecy about the future king of the North who will dominate Egypt and its allied peoples (Daniel 11:43), and in the description of the power of Thebes and its allies (Nahum 3:9). The term always designates a people allied or subordinate to Egypt, never a direct enemy of God or Israel.

sens: Son of Shem, ancestor of the peoples of ancient Lydia
Warrior people or region known for its archers and warriors
Territory located in Asia Minor or North Africa
H3865.detail:
1. Lud is a figure from ancient times, presented as one of the sons of Shem (Genesis 10:22 and 1 Chronicles 1:17), alongside Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, and Aram. Like other names in this genealogical chapter, it also becomes the name of the people or region that his descendants would have founded.
2. Lud designates a people known for its military strength, formidable warriors, and especially its excellent archers. Isaiah 66:19 speaks of "Lud, who draw the bow"; Ezekiel 27:10 states that "those from Persia, Lud, and Put served in your army" and "hung the shield and helmet in your midst."
3. Lud is mentioned alongside other nations, nations with which it shares alliances or ties. In Ezekiel 30:5, Lud is among the allies who "will fall by the sword with them."
H3865.origine: The name Lud literally means "strife," an image of a warrior people. In the Greek Old Testament, the Lydians (derived from Lud) are also called Ludim. The historical territory likely corresponds to ancient Lydia in Asia Minor, a region renowned for its warriors and wealth.
H3865.emploi: Lud appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the context of lists or prophecies. First in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:22 and 1 Chronicles 1:17), where it is listed as a son of Shem. Then, it appears in oracles about nations and military alliances: Isaiah 66:19 includes it among the distant peoples who have not heard of God and to whom His glory will be announced; Ezekiel 27:10 mentions it as a mercenary in the service of a regional power; Ezekiel 30:5 associates it with allies who will face divine judgment.

sens: people from North Africa, descendants of Mitsraïm
H3866G.detail: The Ludim are a people descended from Mitsraïm (Egypt), listed among his descendants in Genesis 10:13 and 1 Chronicles 1:11. They belonged to the ancient peoples of the Mediterranean basin and North Africa, likely related to Lydia or coastal regions of North Africa. This people appears in the genealogy of nations as one of the human groups stemming from Egyptian descent.
H3866G.origine: The word refers to the descendants of Lud, a son of Shem according to some traditions, but the Bible also associates it with an Egyptian people (sons of Mitsraïm). The Hebrew term "Ludim" is the plural that designates the members of this people. The precise identification remains debated among historians, but Hebrew tradition links them to the populations of North Africa and the Mediterranean basin.
H3866G.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible: in Genesis 10:13 and in 1 Chronicles 1:11, both in the context of the genealogies of nations after the Flood. In each occurrence, the Ludim are listed as one of the sons of Mitsraïm, between the Anamim and the Lehabim, in a list of distinct peoples that constitute dispersed humanity. These biblical genealogies serve to situate the known nations within a historical and genealogical framework. The absence of other mentions shows that this people, although known in antiquity, did not play a central narrative role in biblical history.

sens: Person or people descending from Lud, ancestor mentioned in the time of the Patriarchs
H3866H.detail: 1. The Ludim are the descendants of Lud, son of Shem and brother of Asshur, Elam, Arpachshad, and Aram (see Genesis 10:22). The people of Lud is an ethnic group from antiquity, stemming from the same genealogical root, just like the other peoples listed in this genealogy of the sons of Shem.
H3866H.origine: The term Ludian comes from the proper name Lud (לוּד, H3865), son of Shem, mentioned in the genealogical table of Genesis 10. The suffix "-ian" indicates belonging to this ancestral group, according to the classical biblical usage for designating peoples by the name of their founding ancestor.
H3866H.emploi: The term appears only once in the Bible, in the prophet Jeremiah (46:9), where it designates a people allied with Egypt during a military campaign. The context shows that the Ludim were renowned warriors, particularly for their skill with the bow, alongside the Ethiopians and the Putites. This mention confirms that Lud represents a historical people geographically situated in the ancient world, even though its precise location remains debated by historians.
H3866H.portee: This name reminds us how Scripture situates the history of humanity within real genealogies, uniting all peoples in a common descent. For the reader, it is an invitation to recognize the unity of the human race under God's providence and the historical reality of the biblical word.

sens: To be united together, to form a bond
To unite with someone or something
To adhere to a person, a cause, a covenant
H3867A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a union, a bond that brings together: people, nations, or even objects join, gather. It is the image of communion, of shared belonging. In Genesis 29:34, it is the husband who "will attach himself" to his wife, meaning he will be closely united to her.
2. The verb also denotes the action of connecting to someone or a community: in Isaiah 56:6, the foreigners "will attach themselves" to the Lord to serve Him, expressing a personal commitment to follow someone or participate in their cause.
3. Figuratively, it means to adhere to a covenant or a moral and religious commitment: peoples "join" Israel to enter into the Lord's covenant (Isaiah 14:1), or attach themselves to the Sabbath and God's promises (Isaiah 56:3).
H3867A.origine: The Hebrew verb lavah comes from a root that expresses the idea of sticking, of uniting closely. The word belongs to the family of verbs of union and bond: it emphasizes less a complete fusion than a voluntary or necessary adherence, an association. In Numbers 18:4, the Levites are "attached" to the service of the tabernacle, showing that they are linked by their function and duty.
H3867A.emploi: The verb appears twelve times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical and prophetic books. It often expresses a union between people (Genesis 29:34, the marital bond), between nations (Psalms 83:9, nations that ally), or between a person and God (Isaiah 56:6, religious attachment). In covenant contexts, lavah carries a nuance of voluntary adherence and commitment to a cause or divine promise. The verb can also convey a forced or deceptive association (Daniel 11:34, joining hypocritically).
H3867A.portee: This word reminds the reader that biblical faith is not isolated: it implies a union with God and with His people. Attachment to God is not a mere intellectual belief, but a living bond that transforms the one who attaches to it (Isaiah 56:6). It also invites us to discern the quality of our alliances: some arise from sincerity and love, others from calculation or hypocrisy (Daniel 11:34).

sens: To lend money or property to someone with the expectation of it being returned
To receive money or property from another with the obligation to return it
To advance funds as credit
Characterizing one who lends or borrows
H3867B.detail:
1. To lend means to temporarily give a sum of money or property to someone who promises to return it. It is an act of generosity or commerce. In Exodus 22:25, God commands Israel to "lend" money to those in need, without charging interest: it is a loan between brothers, not between creditor and debtor.
2. To borrow is the opposite: to temporarily receive something with the commitment to return it. Psalm 37:21 contrasts the wicked who "borrows" without returning with the one who repays what he owes.
3. At a collective level, to lend also means economic domination: in Deuteronomy 28:12, if Israel obeys, the Lord will grant him prosperity and he "will lend" to many nations (meaning he will dominate them). Conversely, in verse 44, the oppressor "will lend" to Israel and Israel will have to obey him.
4. The righteous "lends" willingly and his generosity is blessed: in Psalms 37:26, the righteous is "compassionate" and "lends," and "his offspring is blessed." This shows that lending reveals the character of the one who does it.
H3867B.origine: The Hebrew verb lâvâh comes from a root that evokes the idea of binding, of engaging. It expresses the mutual obligation between the lender and the borrower: one is bound by his commitment to return, the other by his trust. Related words reinforce this idea of bond and commitment. This word is specifically Hebrew and has no direct equivalent in Greek, although Greek translators chose δανείζω (danéizo) in parallel passages.
H3867B.emploi: This verb appears 10 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in legislative books (Exodus, Deuteronomy) and in wisdom literature (Psalms, Proverbs). It is used in two distinct contexts: first, moral instruction on lending without interest to the poor (Exodus 22:25); secondly, the image of economic domination between nations (Deuteronomy 28:12, 44). In Psalms and Proverbs, the verb takes on a moral hue: the righteous "lends" generously, while the wicked "borrows" without returning. The word always emphasizes either a bond of obligation or a relationship of domination or generosity.
H3867B.portee: This word reminds believers that money is not neutral: lending reveals the character of the one who lends. Lending without interest to the poor is an act of justice, not condescending charity. Conversely, borrowing without returning is a sin. Israel's spiritual prosperity depended on its obedience, which would allow it to "lend" rather than borrow. For today, the Christian sees that wisely managing money and being generous to the needy is a mark of wisdom and justice.

sens: To stray, to turn away from a direction or path
To take a winding, sinuous road that moves away from the straight path
To be perverse, deviating in behavior or thoughts
To become or remain hidden, moving out of sight
H3868.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: to stray or move away from something. One can turn aside their gaze, thoughts, or intentions. It is to voluntarily or involuntarily leave what was in front of oneself (Proverbs 3:21: "Let not these teachings depart from your eyes").
2. In a spatial sense: to take a path that turns, that winds, which is not direct. Instead of walking straight toward the goal, one zigzags, moving away. It is the image of a winding path, the sinuous roads that the foolish take (Proverbs 2:15: "who take crooked paths").
3. In a moral and spiritual sense: this describes a perverse person, who strays from righteousness, whose heart and actions deviate from justice (Proverbs 3:32: "the Lord detests the perverse").
4. The word can also describe something that becomes invisible or hidden, moving out of the field of vision — less common, but the idea remains that of movement that escapes sight.
H3868.origine: The Hebrew root luz expresses the fundamental idea of straying, bending, moving away from a straight line. It paints the image of a path that deviates, of one who turns aside. The word belongs to the family of movement verbs: nuances can be found depending on the verbal forms (simple, passive, causative), but the central image remains that of deviation and distance. This root is used to denote both physical detours and moral waywardness.
H3868.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in Proverbs (5 occurrences) and once in Isaiah. Proverbs uses it to contrast the straight path of wisdom and the fear of God with the crooked path of folly and sin. The "perverse" (the man who follows crooked paths) is presented as an enemy of God and an object of His disdain, while the one who keeps the straight teachings in his heart walks in wisdom. Isaiah uses the same word to describe the "detours" of human politics — the tricks and schemes resorted to instead of trusting God.
H3868.portee: This word teaches an essential spiritual lesson: there is a radical difference between the straight path and the diverted path, between righteousness and perversity. For the Christian reader, it is a call to remain on the straight path of divine wisdom, without being seduced by the apparent detours that promise profit but lead away from God. The word invites honesty, transparency, and caution against human schemes.

sens: Tree with white or pink flowers producing almonds
Wood of this tree, used in crafts and decorations
H3869.detail:
1. The almond tree is a fruit tree known for its beauty and its almonds, a highly valued fruit in the biblical world. In Genesis 30:37, Jacob uses green branches of almond, poplar, and plane trees for an act of livestock selection: he peels white strips that contrast with the bark, creating a remarkable pattern.
2. Almond wood is a noble material, used both for practical purposes and for valuable or ornamental objects. Its natural striped appearance, highlighted by Jacob's peeling, shows that this tree was appreciated for its visual distinction.
H3869.origine: The Hebrew word לוּז (luz) specifically designates the almond tree and its fruit. Its etymology refers to the idea of hardness and solidity, which well evokes the hard shell of the almond. The almond tree, native to the Middle East, was common in the land of Canaan and valued for its hard wood and its oil-rich fruit.
H3869.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 30:37. Jacob chooses almond branches, probably for their contrasting color and distinctive appearance, in the context of his agreement with Laban regarding the division of the flock. This context shows that the almond tree was common enough to be used in daily activities and recognizable by its visual characteristics.
H3869.portee: This passage reminds us that God honors the ingenuity and prudence of His servant Jacob. The almond tree, used by Jacob creatively to mark the flock, illustrates how God guides and blesses those who act wisely in their legitimate endeavors.

sens: city founded in the land of the Hittites
H3870G.detail: Luz is the name of a city built by a man from the tribe of Joseph in the land of the Hittites, after the conquest of Canaan. This name literally means "almond tree" in Hebrew, probably because the region was rich in almond trees or that the tree grew abundantly there (Judges 1:26).
H3870G.origine: The Hebrew word לוּז (luz) means "almond tree" — the tree that produces almonds. It is a concrete name borrowed from nature: it was given to this new city, perhaps because of the local vegetation or to commemorate a remarkable tree in the area. In Canaan, this name or its variants also designated ancient sites.
H3870G.emploi: Luz appears only once in this passage from Judges (Judges 1:26). The text reports that after the capture of Bethel by the tribe of Joseph, a man from this tribe pursued the king of the Hittites who had fled, and in return, he was allowed to build a new city in the land of the Hittites, which was named Luz. This city bears this name to this day when the text was written.
H3870G.portee: This account illustrates how, even after the conquest of Canaan, relationships with neighboring peoples could lead to peace agreements and the establishment of new places. The name Luz, derived from nature, reminds us that biblical cities bore names rich in meaning, often inspired by their environment.

sens: Ancient name of a city in Canaan, later called Bethel
Site of Jacob's altar and pillar in the mountains of Canaan
Territorial boundary between the tribes of Israel
H3870H.detail:
1. Luz is the ancient name of a city located in the mountains of Canaan, in the Promised Land. According to Genesis 28:19, Jacob arrives at this place and erects a stone as a pillar, then calls it Bethel, which means "house of God"; the text specifies that "the city was previously called Luz." This name change marks the spiritual significance of the place for Jacob and his descendants.

2. Luz also refers to the exact site where the altar and pillar that Jacob erected after his vision of the open heaven and the heavenly ladder were located. In Genesis 35:6, Jacob returns there with his family and recognizes the place: "Jacob came to Luz, which is Bethel." In Genesis 48:3, Jacob still remembers: "God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and He blessed me."

3. Luz also appears in the lists of tribal boundaries (Joshua 16:2 and 18:13), serving as a geographical landmark to delineate the lands allocated to the tribe of Ephraim and the house of Joseph during the conquest of the land.
H3870H.origine: The name Luz literally means "almond" in Hebrew, evoking the almond or almond tree that grows in the Holy Land. This geographical name likely reflects a remarkable tree or a characteristic landscape of the place. Bethel, the new name given by Jacob, means "house of God" (Beth = house, El = God), marking the recognition of divine presence in this location. The grounding in nature (the almond tree) thus gives way to a theological name after Jacob's encounter with God.
H3870H.emploi: Luz appears six times in the Old Testament, always as a proper name designating a city in Canaan. Its usage focuses on three contexts: first, the establishment of the site as a place of divine revelation during Jacob's encounter with God (Genesis 28:19 and 35:6), where the new name Bethel is explicitly linked to the old; next, Jacob's memory reflecting on this foundational event (Genesis 48:3); finally, the lists of territorial boundaries and geographical markers during the division of the land among the tribes (Joshua 16:2, 18:13, Judges 1:23). In all cases, Luz and Bethel refer to the same place, Luz being the ancient name used alongside the new name to recall the site's history.
H3870H.portee: Luz illustrates how God transforms ordinary places into sanctuaries of His presence and how faith marks the geographical history of Israel. The name change from Luz to Bethel signifies that encountering God changes our perspective on things and places: what was simply a site named after a tree becomes the "place where God dwells." For the modern reader, this reminds us that any place can become a space of revelation and communion with the Lord.

sens: Flat and rigid surface of stone, wood, or metal, shaped or crafted to serve as support
Wooden board, platform, or construction element in religious or civil structures
Surface on which a message, document, or law is engraved or written
Figuratively, the heart or mind of man as the place where God's will is inscribed
H3871.detail:
1. A table can be a piece of carved stone, wood, or metal. The passage in Exodus 24:12 refers to the stone tablets that God gave to Moses on Sinai: rigid surfaces intended to bear something important. Exodus 38:7 describes how wooden boards were used to make the altar of worship.
2. In construction, boards and tables are shaped or assembled to form structures. It is a functional element, sometimes ornate, but primarily useful: to support, divide, create a working surface or platform.
3. The table becomes the ideal support for engraving, writing, or inscribing. The two stone tablets bore the ten words of the covenant (Exodus 31:18). Habakkuk 2:2 calls for a vision to be engraved on tablets so that the one who reads it may run. Isaiah 30:8 commands to write a word on a tablet for testimony.
4. Proverbs 3:3 transposes this meaning: "Let not mercy and truth forsake you; bind them around your neck, write them on the tablet of your heart." The image of the tablets becomes that of the mind or heart where God's law is inscribed, no longer engraved in stone but in the believer's inner being.
H3871.origine: The Hebrew word לוּחַ comes from a root that evokes the idea of carving, engraving, shaping a flat surface. It primarily designates a shaped object, a rigid and flat piece. The root is related to the action of tracing or dividing. In Proverbs, the word transitions from the concrete sense (material object) to the figurative sense (the heart or mind as a surface where divine wisdom or law is inscribed).
H3871.emploi: This word appears 33 times in the Hebrew Bible. It primarily designates the two stone tablets on which God engraved the ten commandments (Exodus 24:12, 31:18, 34:1-4; Deuteronomy 9-10). Moses broke them in his anger (Exodus 32:19) upon seeing the golden calf, then received them a second time. They were placed in the Ark of the Covenant (1 Kings 8:9; 2 Chronicles 5:10). The word also applies to the wooden boards used to construct the altar and its accessories (Exodus 27:8, 38:7). In the prophetic and wisdom literature, it takes on a figurative meaning: Habakkuk 2:2 orders to engrave a vision on tablets, Isaiah 30:8 calls to write a testimony on a tablet, and Jeremiah 17:1 denounces the transgression engraved with a diamond point on the tablet of the heart. Proverbs 3:3 and 7:3 transfer the image to the commandments or wisdom to be inscribed in the heart.
H3871.portee: For the believer, the stone tablets remind us that God has inscribed His will and covenant in a visible, solid, and transmissible manner. The image extends spiritually: God's law is not just an external text; it must be inscribed in the heart (Proverbs 3:3). This transition from material tablets to the tablets of the heart prepares the Christian understanding of the New Testament: God writes His law not on stone, but in the minds and hearts of those who trust Him.

sens: City of Moab located south of the Arnon River
H3872.detail: Luchith is a city in the kingdom of Moab, a region located east of the Dead Sea. Its name means "tablets" or "heights," suggesting a mountainous site. The Bible mentions it only in prophetic passages describing the destruction and flight of Moab: in Isaiah 15:5 and Jeremiah 48:5, we see the Moabites ascending the way to Luchith weeping, fleeing before an army. This city thus marked a well-known route, a mountain passage that one had to necessarily traverse to flee north or south.
H3872.origine: The name Luchith comes from a Hebrew root meaning "tablet" or "plateau," suggesting a site with flat or well-defined heights. This type of geographical name was common in the Holy Land to designate places recognizable by their relief. No other occurrence of the word itself is found in the Old Testament, but the root evokes the idea of regular or elevated surfaces.
H3872.emploi: Luchith appears only twice in the Bible. In Isaiah 15:5 and Jeremiah 48:5, it appears in prophetic oracles against Moab, both describing the Moabite fugitives who ascend the way to Luchith while shedding tears. These two prophecies, although slightly different in their wording, speak of the same drama: the desperate flight of the inhabitants before an invasion. Luchith thus becomes a symbol of a route of distress and mourning, through which the people are condemned to exile or destruction.

sens: Man who lived during the time of the exile and the return of Israel to Jerusalem
H3873.detail: Hallochesch is a man mentioned twice in the book of Nehemiah, during the time of the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. His son Shallum is presented as the leader of half of the district of Jerusalem and participated in the rebuilding of the walls (Nehemiah 3:12). Hallochesch himself appears among those who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah, committing the people to live according to God's Law (Nehemiah 10:24).
H3873.origine: The name Hallochesch means "the whisperer" or "one who whispers," from the Hebrew verb that denotes the action of speaking softly, mysteriously. This type of name, formed from an action or characteristic, was common in ancient Israel.
H3873.emploi: Hallochesch appears twice in Nehemiah, both times at the moment of the return of the exiles from Babylon (around the 5th century BCE). He is first known as the father of Shallum, who oversaw the reconstruction of an important section of the walls of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:12). A few chapters later, Hallochesch himself is listed among the leaders of the people who signed or sealed Nehemiah's covenant, promising to observe the Law of the Lord (Nehemiah 10:24). He represents those influential families of Jerusalem who participated in the spiritual and physical restoration of the city.

sens: Completely cover something with a fabric or garment to protect or hide it
Cover the face or body with a garment out of modesty, fear, or mourning
Figuratively: to veil, mask, or hide something in a way that removes it from sight or understanding
H3874.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to cover or wrap an object completely in fabric to protect or preserve it. In 1 Samuel 21:9, Goliath's sword is "wrapped" in a cloth, kept aside and protected.
2. The word can also describe the action of covering oneself with a garment to conceal or express an emotion. When Elijah hears the voice of God (1 Kings 19:13), he "wraps" his face in his cloak — a gesture of respect mixed with fear before the divine.
3. Figuratively, the word denotes what hides or veils a reality. In Isaiah 25:7, the "veil" that "covers" all peoples is what prevents them from seeing the clarity of God's purpose, obscuring their understanding.
H3874.origine: The Hebrew verb לוּט (lut) comes from a root that evokes the idea of wrapping or tightening around. It is a simple and concrete word, related to the physical act of covering. The Hebrew language often uses this type of verb to transition from a material meaning to a figurative one: covering an object becomes "hiding a truth." The word belongs to the ordinary vocabulary of daily life.
H3874.emploi: The verb lut appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. The first two uses (1 Samuel 21:9 and 1 Kings 19:13) are concrete: the sword wrapped in a cloth, Elijah wrapping his face. The third (Isaiah 25:7) generalizes the meaning toward the idea of moral or spiritual veiling — the veil that covers all peoples. This progression from the concrete to the figurative shows how ancient Israelites thought: the physical gesture becomes the image of a spiritual reality. In all cases, "to wrap" speaks of something that is hidden, protected, or removed from view.
H3874.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to reflect on what veils or reveals divine truth. In Isaiah 25:7, the context of future salvation shows that God will remove the veils that prevent humanity from seeing Him. For Elijah, wrapping his face expresses a posture of humility and reverence before God. This verb reminds us that the relationship with God involves visible gestures — covering oneself, uncovering oneself — that express inner reality.

sens: Piece of fabric that covers and hides
What envelops or masks something
Invisible barrier that separates or obscures
H3875.detail:
1. The word denotes a piece of fabric, a covering that conceals or protects something. In Isaiah 25:7, it refers to a veil that covers all peoples, a thick covering that envelops them.
2. Figuratively, the veil represents what masks, obscures vision or understanding. It is an invisible barrier that prevents peoples from seeing or knowing something.
3. Metaphorically, it is what separates, what isolates: the veil spoken of in Isaiah is a covering of darkness or ignorance that envelops the nations before God destroys it.
H3875.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that expresses the idea of covering, enveloping, or concealing. It belongs to the family of terms that describe an action of dissimulation or protection by a fabric. The image is that of a cloth or linen that extends over something to hide it.
H3875.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 25:7. It poetically and symbolically describes a veil or covering that envelops all peoples and nations. In this prophetic context, God promises to destroy this veil that obscures the peoples, the veil of ignorance or judgment. It is an image of liberation and illumination for all nations.
H3875.portee: This passage reminds us that sin and ignorance of God form a barrier between God and humanity. Isaiah's promise is one of future revelation: God will remove the veil that blinds the peoples. For the believer, this speaks to God's role in removing our spiritual blindness and bringing us to the truth. It is a word of hope: no veil can withstand God.

sens: The son of Haran and nephew of Abraham
The man who traveled with Abraham in the land of Canaan
The resident of Sodom who welcomed the angels
The survivor of the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah
H3876.detail: 1. Lot is the son of Haran, the brother of Abraham, making him Abraham's nephew — he belongs to the generation of the patriarchs and is first mentioned in the genealogy of Terach (Genesis 11:27). 2. Lot first traveled with Abraham from Ur to Canaan, also possessing livestock, sheep, and tents (Genesis 13:5-6); however, as their wealth increased and their herdsmen quarreled, Abraham and Lot separated — Lot chose for himself the plain of the Jordan and settled in Sodom (Genesis 13:10-12). 3. In Sodom, Lot became an established man and welcomed two angels sent to check on the wickedness of the city, inviting them to his home and protecting them from the men of Sodom who wanted to know them carnally (Genesis 19:1-10). 4. During the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, God, remembering Abraham, saved Lot and his two daughters by allowing them to flee the city before it was consumed by fire (Genesis 19:23-29) — Lot took refuge in Zoar and then in a cave with his daughters.
H3876.origine: The name "Lot" means "veil" or "covering" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of something that envelops or conceals. Lot appears exclusively in the Pentateuch and the Psalms as a specific historical figure, without nominal derivatives. His story illustrates how a man can be saved by his proximity to one who walks with God (Abraham) and by God's own merciful judgment.
H3876.emploi: Lot is mentioned 32 times in the Bible, primarily in Genesis (from 11:27 to 19:37) and briefly in Deuteronomy and Psalms. He first appears as Abraham's companion in his calling (Genesis 11:27 to 13:12), then as a resident of Sodom where he acquires a social position: he sits at the city gate and welcomes visitors (Genesis 19:1). His role culminates when he becomes a witness and beneficiary of the destruction of Sodom, saved because of his relationship to Abraham. After his rescue, the Bible mentions his descendants — Moab and Ben-Ammi, ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites — and these peoples appear in later references (Deuteronomy 2:9, 2:19). His story illustrates the contrast between one who chooses according to his eyes and desires (the plain of the Jordan) and one who obeys the divine call.
H3876.portee: The story of Lot teaches that salvation does not depend solely on personal righteousness, but on God's grace and the role of intercession — Abraham prayed for Lot, and God spared him "because of Abraham" (Genesis 19:29). It also shows how surrounding sin gradually corrupts: Lot initially distanced himself from Abraham by choosing Sodom, then became so absorbed by the city that his sons-in-law no longer listened to him (Genesis 19:14). For the believer, it reminds us of the importance of remaining separate from evil and placing our trust in God rather than in visible riches.

sens: Horite chief during the Patriarchs' era
Eldest son of Seir the Horite
Tribal chief of the unusual peoples of Canaan
H3877.detail: Lothan is a Horite chief mentioned in the genealogy of the peoples who occupied Canaan before the arrival of Israel. He is presented as the eldest son of Seir the Horite (Genesis 36:20), a central figure among the ancient inhabitants of the land. Lothan had two sons, Hori and Hemam, and a sister named Timna (Genesis 36:22). He is listed among the Horite chiefs who dominated the region (Genesis 36:29), attesting to his status and authority in his community.
H3877.origine: The name Lothan means "covering" in Hebrew, perhaps alluding to his protection or his role as a covering for his tribe. Lothan belongs to the lineage of Seir the Horite, a people who controlled the mountains of Edom before the arrival of the descendants of Esau. The Horites formed a civilization whose genealogical traces the Bible has preserved, particularly in the account of Genesis 36.
H3877.emploi: Lothan appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, all in genealogies: twice in Genesis 36 (verses 20, 22, and 29) and twice in 1 Chronicles 1 (verses 38 and 39). These passages present his genealogy in a very similar manner, confirming his role as an important genealogical figure. There are no accounts of actions or specific events concerning him: Lothan appears solely as a link in the chain of peoples who populated Canaan before Israel.

sens: son of Jacob and Leah, ancestor of the tribe of Levi
H3878.detail: 1. Levi is the third son that Leah bore to Jacob. According to Genesis 29:34, Leah gave him this name saying: "This time my husband will be attached to me" — the name means "attached to" or "joined to." Levi had four sons: Gershom, Kohath, Merari, and Jochebed, whose descendants formed the tribe of Levi (1 Chronicles 6:16). Unlike his brothers, Levi did not receive a territory of his own in Canaan: his descendants were dispersed among the other tribes to serve in worship (Deuteronomy 10:8).
H3878.origine: The name Levi comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to attach" or "to join." Leah chose this name hoping that her husband would become more closely bonded to her after the birth of this third son. The tribe that descends from Levi — called the tribe of Levi or the Levites — bears his name and receives a unique religious function in Israel: it is consecrated to the service of the temple and to assist the priests.
H3878.emploi: Levi is first mentioned at his birth in Genesis 29:34. He is then listed as one of Jacob's twelve sons in genealogical lists (Genesis 35:23; Exodus 1:2; 1 Chronicles 2:1). The majority of the uses of the name "Levi" in the Bible concern his descendants: the term "sons of Levi" or "children of Levi" is used to refer to the entire tribe and its cultic functions. This tribe is chosen by God for the service of the sanctuary (Numbers 3:15-17; Deuteronomy 10:8), to offer sacrifices and bless Israel (Deuteronomy 21:5). After entering Canaan, the Levites received cities but no tribal territory, subsisting on the tithes brought by Israel (Numbers 18:21; Deuteronomy 18:1).
H3878.portee: Levi embodies the principle of consecration: his entire lineage is set apart, not to dominate, but to serve. This reminds the reader that true greatness lies in obedience to God's call, even when it challenges human expectations. The fate of the Levites shows that God has specific plans for those He chooses, and that faith is measured by the acceptance of these designs.

sens: member of the tribe of Levi, son of Jacob
assistant to the priests in the service of the temple
singer or musician in worship
guardian or servant of the sanctuary
H3879.detail:
1. A Levite is a member of the tribe of Levi, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. Levi was the third son of Jacob and Leah (Genesis 29:34). His descendants form a special lineage within the people of Israel.

2. From the time of the desert, the Levites receive a special mission: to serve God and assist the priests in the worship of the temple. They do not receive a territorial inheritance like the other tribes, but cities and portions of the offerings (Numbers 18).

3. The Levites perform various functions: some sing and play music during celebrations, as shown in Ezra 6:18 where "the Levites" are appointed "for the service of God in Jerusalem." Others guard the temple gates or ensure its maintenance.

4. These servants of the sanctuary enjoy an honored position but are distinct from the priests. Ezra 7:24 clearly distinguishes "the priests, the Levites, the singers, the gatekeepers," showing the varied roles they occupy in the service of God's house.
H3879.origine: The word Levite comes from the name Levi, which means "attached" or "joined" in Hebrew — an image of one who is devoted to the service of God. The name of the tribe thus applies to all its descendants. The structure of the Levitical tribe traces back to Levi's three sons: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, each founding their branch with specific functions in worship.
H3879.emploi: The word "Levite" appears four times in the book of Ezra, which recounts Israel's return from exile in Babylon around 538 B.C. In these texts, the Levites are mentioned alongside the priests and the people: in Ezra 6:16, they participate together in the dedication of the rebuilt temple "with joy." In Ezra 6:18 and 7:13, they are listed among those whom King Cyrus allows to go to Jerusalem. In Ezra 7:24, they benefit from royal tax exemptions, just like the priests. These mentions show that the Levites form an organized and recognized body, integral to the religious and communal life of Israel.
H3879.portee: Discovering the role of the Levites reminds Christians that the service of God is not reserved for a distant elite, but concerns the entire people. Each Levite, according to his function — singer, gatekeeper, servant — contributes to the praise and holiness of worship. For today's believer, it is an invitation to recognize that all members of the Church are called to serve, according to the gifts that God has entrusted to them (1 Peter 4:10).

sens: ornament woven to be worn on the head
honorary distinction, mark of dignity
reward or glory given to one who is worthy
H3880.detail:
1. The crown is an ornament that is woven or shaped to be placed on the head. It is a decoration of grace, as shown in Proverbs 1:9 where wisdom becomes a crown that the father desires for his son.
2. It symbolizes the honor and dignity of the one who wears it. In Proverbs 4:9, the one who speaks (wisdom) promises her disciple to crown him with a crown of grace: a visible and recognizable distinction.
3. It is also a reward for behavior and life choices. Receiving this crown means being exalted, placed in the forefront, marked as precious and approved.
H3880.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that evokes intertwining, weaving. In Hebrew, a crown can be simply braided or adorned, but it always evokes the idea of surrounding, encircling, marking the top. It is an object of prestige in all ancient cultures.
H3880.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the Book of Proverbs. It refers to the crown of grace that wisdom promises to those who listen to and follow her. It is a poetic image: wisdom does not give a crown in the literal sense, but elevates the one who wears it, making him honorable and worthy. The context is always one of personal honor and moral reward.
H3880.portee: This word speaks to the Christian about the dignity received in seeking wisdom and virtue. The crown is not a prize that is seized by force, but an adornment that the choice of good confers upon us. It reminds us that living according to divine wisdom is not a burden, but an elevation, a discreet yet real glorification of the one who engages in it.

sens: member of the tribe of Levi, one of the twelve tribes of Israel
man consecrated to the service of worship and the sanctuary of God
H3881.detail: 1. Levite primarily refers to a descendant of Levi, the third son of Jacob and Leah (Genesis 29:34). The Levites form an entire tribe among the twelve tribes of Israel, with their own families and clans (Numbers 3:20). 2. The term mainly applies to their religious role: God chose them to serve in the sanctuary and assist the priests. They guard the Tent of Meeting, transport the sacred furnishings, sing during services, and receive the tithe in exchange for this service (Numbers 18:23-24). Unlike other Israelites, they do not own land in Israel, as their inheritance is the Lord Himself and the worship rendered to Him (Deuteronomy 10:9; Numbers 35:2-8 for their cities of refuge).
H3881.origine: The Hebrew word לֵוִי (Levi) etymologically means "attached" or "joined" — the idea of being united, incorporated. Leah gave this name to her son saying, "Perhaps now my husband will attach himself to me" (Genesis 29:34). The name thus evokes this union. The Levites bear this name as descendants of Levi, and they are indeed "attached" to the service of God and the sanctuary, forming a specialized class in Israelite worship.
H3881.emploi: The word appears 263 times in the Bible. It is found predominantly in the books of the Pentateuch (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy), which describe the organization and duties of the Levites. It is also frequent in the historical books (Joshua, 1-2 Chronicles) and in Nehemiah. The Levites always appear in connection with religious service: they are arranged around the sanctuary (Numbers 1:50-53), receive instruction in worship (Numbers 8:6-22), collect the tithe, guard the temple gates, and participate in solemn feasts (2 Chronicles 30:27; Nehemiah 7:73).
H3881.portee: For a Christian reader, the Levites illustrate the idea that a people can be consecrated to the service of God. Their consecration — they are "attached" to God — shows how God establishes a holy distinction between the profane and the sacred, and how He provides for the maintenance of those who serve Him. The Epistle to the Hebrews relates the Levitical priesthood to Christ, who is the Great High Priest. Thus, the Levites help to understand what Jesus accomplishes once for all.

sens: Aquatic monster from ancient mythology, a feared sea creature
Large aquatic animal, possibly a crocodile or a giant reptile
Mythical or legendary creature, symbol of raw and chaotic power
Adversary of the Creator God, a hostile force that God dominates
H3882.detail:
1. Leviathan is a prodigious sea creature, famous in Near Eastern legends. Biblical texts describe it as a monster of terrifying power, possibly a large aquatic animal like a crocodile, or a mythical creature whose exact identity eludes us (Job 40:20 places it among the animals created by God).
2. The Bible mentions it as a living being, captured or mastered by the Lord: in Psalm 74:14, God "breaks the heads of Leviathan" on behalf of His people.
3. It is a figure of rebellion and chaos: in Isaiah 27:1, the prophet announces that "the Lord will punish with His fierce, great, and strong sword Leviathan, the fleeing serpent, Leviathan, the twisting serpent."
4. Leviathan symbolizes all power hostile to God — threatening, capricious, but ultimately defeated by the Creator God. It embodies the ordering of primordial chaos.
H3882.origine: The Hebrew name לִוְיָתָן (liv'yatan) is ancient and also appears in Canaanite and Phoenician mythologies in similar forms. Its exact etymology is debated, but it may evoke the idea of "twisting" or "rolling" (that which twists, that which undulates). In Psalm 104:26, Leviathan is simply an animal that God created to play in the seas — the image humanizes: the creature becomes a part of the divine harmony of creation.
H3882.emploi: Leviathan appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts that emphasize its power. It is treated both as a real animal (Job 40:20, where it is asked if one can "take it with hooks"), and as a cosmic force defeated by God (Psalms 74:14, Isaiah 27:1). In Job 3:8, Leviathan is called to "trouble" the day of Job's birth, as if it were a power capable of cursing. It is always a creature linked to aquatic chaos, the mystery of the depths, but never beyond the power of God: it is God who made it, God who contains it, God who will conquer it.
H3882.portee: Leviathan reminds the believer that God's omnipotence is not threatened by any force, even the most terrifying or chaotic. This prodigious creature, whose true nature we do not even know, remains under the divine hand. It speaks to those who suffer or doubt: the apparent chaos of the world, the absurdity or hostility that crushes us, are known and dominated by the Creator God. Leviathan is also an invitation to humility: to recognize that there are mysteries we do not understand, but that God masters them.

sens: set of steps allowing ascent or descent
spiral staircase or enclosed in a narrow space
vertical passage or conduit in a structure
H3883.detail:
1. The word designates a staircase, that is, a series of steps that allow passage from one level to another. It is a practical and concrete architectural element.
2. The staircase described here is particularly a spiral or enclosed staircase, likely in a tight space, evoking a compact structure, perhaps an emergency staircase or a discreet passage inside a building.
3. The word can also evoke a conduit or a vertical shaft dug into a structure to allow passage — the image is that of an upward way arranged within the very thickness of a construction.
H3883.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of turning or wrapping around a central axis. The word literally designates a spiral staircase, that is, steps that turn around a pivot or wrap in a narrow space, as seen in towers or massive structures. It is a specialized term of sacred architecture.
H3883.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 6:8, where it designates the spiral staircase of Solomon's temple. It is precisely the staircase by which one accessed the upper floors of the sanctuary. This unique context shows that it is a precise architectural term, used to describe a specific part of an important sacred building. Its use in this context emphasizes the care and complexity brought to the construction of the temple.
H3883.portee: This word reminds us that Solomon's temple was a remarkably constructed building, with particular attention to architectural details. For the reader, it illustrates the glory and grandeur of the worship rendered to God in the Old Testament, as well as the excellence put into the realization of what was intended to honor the Lord.

sens: Negative condition: what would happen if something did not occur
Concession: acknowledging that a single thing prevents something from happening
Indirect affirmation: strongly affirming the existence or importance of something by denying the opposite
H3884.detail:
1. Negative condition: the word introduces a condition contrary to reality, to express what would occur without an obstacle. It is the negative form of a supposition: "if this had not happened, then..." Jacob tells Laban in Genesis 31:42: "If the God of my father had not been with me... you would have now sent me away empty" — he affirms that without divine protection, he would have been ruined.
2. Concession: the word highlights a single reason that prevents something from happening. Elisha refuses to pay attention to the king of Israel in 2 Kings 3:14: "If I did not regard Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, I would not pay any attention to you" — it is only for Jehoshaphat that he intervenes.
3. Indirect affirmation: by strongly denying the opposite, the phrase affirms something with certainty. David cries in Psalms 94:17: "If the Lord had not been my help, my soul would soon have dwelt in silence" — this means with certainty that God is his help.
H3884.origine: The word is a negative conditional conjunction formed from a root meaning "to prevent" or "to restrain." It combines the idea of a condition with a negation: "unless" or "if not." This construction is characteristic of biblical Hebrew, which loves to express certainty by passing through the negation of the opposite — a very vivid and convincing Semitic way of thinking.
H3884.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the Psalms (6 times) and the historical books. It almost always expresses a condition contrary to reality — something that did not happen, and whose absence is emphasized to show that without it, a misfortune would have occurred. The contexts vary: divine protection (Psalms 94:17, Psalms 119:92), personal intervention (1 Samuel 25:34, 2 Kings 3:14), or divine judgment withheld (Psalms 106:23, Isaiah 1:9). Each time, the meaning remains stable: "if this had not happened, then this would have occurred."
H3884.portee: This word teaches the reader a fundamental biblical wisdom: to recognize what saves us. By using this strong negative form, the biblical authors invite the believer to become aware of what they owe to God alone — His protection, His law, His intervention. It is a way to awaken gratitude and dependence on God: we understand our need by measuring what we would lack without Him.

sens: Stop somewhere to sleep
Stay, remain for a certain time
Dwell, have one's residence (figurative sense)
Let rest, spend the night
H3885A.detail:
1. The primary and most concrete meaning: to stop in a place to sleep. This is what Abraham offers to his visitors in Genesis 19:2: "Spend the night in the house of your servant." Ruth also says to Boaz: "Spend the night here" (Ruth 3:13). This reflects the hospitality of the Old Testament: offering someone shelter for the night.
2. The word extends to the idea of staying, remaining for a certain time in a place, without necessarily sleeping there. In Judges 19:6, the father says to the husband: "Decide to spend the night, and let your heart be merry," which means to stay and enjoy the company.
3. In a figurative sense, the word denotes habitation, the act of residing or having one's dwelling. Psalm 91:1 says: "He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty": this is finding refuge and protection with God.
4. The word can also mean "to spend the night" or "to let rest," particularly in Leviticus 19:13: "You shall not keep the wages of a hired man overnight," meaning do not keep the money with you overnight — pay without delay.
H3885A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of stopping and resting. It is related to the notions of stay and temporary halt. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), the Greek word used is often "koitazô" or "aulizomai," which retain the image of a nighttime rest. The family of the word includes terms designating the night itself and the rest that accompanies it.
H3885A.emploi: The word appears 65 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in historical narratives and wisdom literature. It is found very often in Genesis and Judges, where it describes journeys and stops (Genesis 28:11 "Jacob spent the night in that place," Judges 19 where the night becomes a dramatic motif). In the Psalms and Proverbs, it takes on a theological hue: dwelling or resting under the protection of God (Psalm 91:1). In Leviticus and Exodus, it enters into legal prescriptions regarding the timing of offerings or payments: certain things must not "spend the night." The verb adapts to the context: literal when it concerns travel, figurative when it concerns the relationship with God.
H3885A.portee: For the believer, this simple word opens a profound truth: finding shelter and protection. When the Psalms speak of "dwelling" under the shadow of the Most High, they promise not an absence of danger, but a reassuring presence in the heart of the night — a biblical image of fear and trouble. It is an invitation to see God as a stable, not temporary, refuge. The word also reminds us of hospitality: in biblical culture, offering shelter for the night is a fundamental act of charity.

sens: to express dissatisfaction in a low or restrained voice
to complain against someone
to contest the authority of God or a leader
H3885B.detail:
1. To murmur is to express dissatisfaction through low, muffled words, like a stifled complaint. It is less than a cry of revolt: it is to whisper one's frustration. In the desert, when the Israelites lack water, "the people murmured against Moses" (Exodus 15:24) — they do not openly revolt, but express their worry and reproach by mumbling.
2. To murmur becomes a form of disobedience: one contests those who command us. "Why have you brought us up out of Egypt?" (Exodus 17:3) — the people not only contest the circumstances but challenge the decision of their leader. The Israelites "murmured against me," says God (Numbers 14:27), because they refused to trust Him.
3. At its core, to murmur is to doubt God, to be suspicious of His goodness. When one murmurs, one implicitly says: "God does not love me, God does not know what He is doing." This is why God takes murmuring so seriously — because it reveals a lack of faith.
H3885B.origine: The Hebrew verb lun describes the muffled sound of complaint, similar to the noise made by the human throat when it grumbles — hence the image of murmuring. The Bible uses it almost exclusively to speak of complaints directed at God or at those acting in God's name. It is a word that emphasizes less violent revolt than the gnawing doubt, the contestation of hearts.
H3885B.emploi: This verb appears 14 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the desert narratives (Exodus and Numbers). The Israelites murmur against Moses and Aaron because they are hungry, thirsty, afraid (Exodus 15:24; 16:7; 17:3; Numbers 14:27; 16:41). God hears their murmurs and judges them: it is a symptom of their unbelief. The word also appears in Joshua 9:18, when Israel protests against a treaty, and in Psalm 59:16, where the psalmist says he will sing rather than murmur. Throughout its uses, the meaning remains the same: it is always a complaint that contests or doubts.
H3885B.portee: Murmuring teaches us that our hidden words, our small complaints, our stifled doubts, do not escape us — God hears them (Exodus 16:7-8). To murmur reveals what lies deep in the heart: the absence of trust. In reading these narratives, the Christian learns to view their inner murmurs as signs of unbelief to be fought through prayer and gratitude.

sens: To make something go down one's throat, into one's belly
In a figurative sense, to absorb or endure something without protest
H3886A.detail:
1. To swallow is to move something from the mouth to the stomach, this natural movement of the throat that allows one to ingest food or drink. In Obadiah 1:16, the nations "will drink" and "swallow": the image is of people who are satiated, who gulp down, who consume endlessly, absorbing everything in their path like fire devours wood.
2. In a figurative sense, the verb means to accept or endure something without revolt — to swallow it like a bitter pill. In the same verse in Obadiah, the enemies who drank on the holy mountain of Jerusalem "will swallow" in turn what they have poured out: they will bear the consequences, they will ingest their own judgment.
H3886A.origine: The Hebrew verb לוּעַ comes from a root that describes the movement of the throat and esophagus. It is a concrete word that depicts the physical action before enriching itself with figurative meanings. The family of this word in Hebrew has few derivatives, but the image remains that of ingestion, of absorption.
H3886A.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Obadiah 1:16, where it reinforces the idea of consumption and suffering one's own judgment. The prophet Obadiah announces to the Edomites that they will drink the cup they have poured out on Judah. The usage is highly metaphorical: "to swallow" symbolizes here not only the physical act of drinking but especially the forced acceptance of the consequences of their actions. It is an action verb that emphasizes the irrevocability of judgment.
H3886A.portee: This word reminds us that the evil we pour out on others ultimately returns to us — a classic biblical image of judgment and divine retribution. For the believer, it is an invitation to remember that God does not leave injustices unpunished: whoever has drunk the poison will swallow it sooner or later.

sens: Unreasonable words, impassioned or incoherent speech
A state of mind that drives one to speak without reason or measure
H3886B.detail:
1. The word refers to words that come out of the mouth without restraint or wisdom, like a torrent of empty or disordered speech. Job uses it when he says that his pain is so great that he cannot help but speak in an exaggerated and unrestrained manner (Job 6:3).
2. It is also the inner state that produces these words — when grief, anger, or agitation of the soul overwhelm reason and cause words to flow without a filter. Job confesses that his suffering drives him to say things that may seem foolish to others.
H3886B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of wasting or overturning: to speak of folly is to let flow out of oneself words of no value, as one would pour something out in vain. It is a rare term in biblical Hebrew, emphasizing the exceptional nature of the situation — only extreme pain can drive a wise man like Job to speak this way.
H3886B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 6:3. Job is grappling with unimaginable suffering: his friends accuse him of his accusations against God, and he defends himself by saying that his pain is so heavy and overwhelming that it justifies the apparent excess of his words. He implicitly acknowledges that he has spoken in an unusual manner, but he gives the reason: the weight of his affliction.
H3886B.portee: This word shows us that even the righteous, when tested, can experience a temptation to speak in an impassioned or exaggerated manner. Job does not renounce his moral integrity — he appeals to reason and justice — but he humanly acknowledges that suffering can affect our words. It is a reminder that in the face of extreme pain, compassion should prevail over judgment.

sens: To mock someone, in word or attitude, with disdain or contempt
To speak arrogantly, to boast, to show insolence
To interpret, translate, serve as an intermediary in communication
To make faces, to mimic in order to ridicule
H3887.detail:
1. To mock means to ridicule someone through words or gestures full of contempt. It is to laugh at them to humiliate them. A mocker is one who takes pleasure in this attitude: in Proverbs 1:22, mockers are ranked among sinners, and in Psalms 1:1, the righteous must stay away from their company.
2. To mock also expresses a form of insolence and pride: to speak arrogantly, to boast of one's superiority. In Proverbs 21:24, the mocker is described as haughty and impetuous, acting with "the fury of arrogance."
3. The verb also has the technical meaning of "to serve as an interpreter" or "to translate": in Genesis 42:23, Joseph uses an interpreter to speak with his brothers, as if he did not understand their language.
4. To make faces, to contort one's face to ridicule someone: this concrete image of the mocker distorting their features reflects their contemptible heart.
H3887.origine: The Hebrew verb luts evokes the idea of turning to derision and contempt. The root suggests an action that pushes away, that refuses — that of the mocker who rejects with disdain. In the sense of interpreter, the word expresses one who "translates" or "conveys" the meaning from one language to another. Close variants (like latsats) reinforce this notion of derision. The Septuagint, the ancient Greek version of the Old Testament, uses the word "mocker" for most of these usages.
H3887.emploi: This verb appears 27 times in the Bible, mostly in Proverbs and Psalms. It primarily designates the mocker as a type of sinner: someone who rejects instruction and wisdom, who even scorns correction (Proverbs 9:7-8, 14:6). Mockery is presented as a serious sin that provokes divine anger and indignation (Proverbs 3:34). In parallel, the verb applies to one who interprets or translates: in Genesis 42:23, it is the interpreter who conveys the words; Job 33:23 mentions the "intercessor," a figure of the intermediary. In Isaiah and Psalms, mockery becomes a weapon against the righteous: in Psalms 119:51, mockers persecute the one who keeps the Law.
H3887.portee: Understanding the meaning of "mock" helps the reader see that derision is never trivial before God: it is a refusal of wisdom and humility. The Bible treats the mocker with severity, as they close their heart to instruction. For the Christian, it is a call to flee this attitude of arrogance and contempt, and to instead welcome fraternal correction as a gift.

sens: To work flour and water with the hands to make a dough for baking
To prepare bread or cakes by kneading the flour
Figuratively, to ferment or transform slowly
H3888.detail:
1. To knead means to mix flour and water with the hands to form a uniform dough that will be baked later. It is the fundamental gesture of bread-making: Abraham instructs Sarah to "knead" three measures of fine flour (Genesis 18:6), and the woman who shelters Saul slaughters a calf and "kneads" the flour to make unleavened bread (1 Samuel 28:24).
2. More broadly, the word refers to the act of preparing bread or cakes by kneading the dough. Tamar "kneads" a dough and prepares cakes in front of her brother (2 Samuel 13:8), and the women "knead" the dough to make cakes offered to the queen of heaven (Jeremiah 7:18).
3. Figuratively or in a poetic image, kneading also evokes fermentation and transformation: the baker "kneads" the dough and then lets it rise (Hosea 7:4), suggesting a process of gradual transformation.
H3888.origine: The Hebrew verb lush comes from the root that evokes the action of kneading, of working a soft material with the hands. Its semantic field is very concrete: it always applies to the preparation of food dough, never to other materials. It is a word rooted in the domestic and artisanal life of ancient Israel.
H3888.emploi: The verb lush appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in culinary preparation contexts. It is found mainly in narratives: Abraham asks for the flour to be kneaded to welcome his visitors (Genesis 18:6), Saul's wife quickly prepares a meal by kneading the dough (1 Samuel 28:24), Tamar cooks for her brother by kneading dough (2 Samuel 13:8). The prophet Jeremiah uses it to describe the idolatrous worship practices of women who knead the dough for cakes offered to the queen of heaven (Jeremiah 7:18). Hosea uses the verb in a comparison that evokes the process of fermentation (Hosea 7:4). The word remains firmly anchored in its literal and concrete meaning.
H3888.portee: Kneading dough is a simple and ordinary image of domestic preparation. It reminds us that in the Bible, everyday gestures — preparing food, welcoming, serving — carry spiritual weight and relate to hospitality and service. These verses also show how the work of hands, even the most humble, is woven into the fabric of human relationships and relationships with God.

sens: near someone, in the vicinity
at someone's home
in someone's company
H3890.detail:
1. The word primarily expresses spatial proximity: being at someone's place means being near them, in the same location. In Ezra 4:12, "the Jews who left your place" refers to those who left the king of Persia to go to Jerusalem: it concerns those who were in his presence or under his authority.
2. The word also evokes the home, the household: at someone's place means at their house, in their domestic or personal space.
3. The meaning extends to companionship, to relationship: being at someone's place means living with them, sharing their life or plans.
This simple yet rich preposition allows for discussion of human proximity in all its aspects.
H3890.origine: This Hebrew preposition is formed on the idea of movement toward or proximity with. It is related to roots that express accompaniment and presence. In biblical Hebrew, it functions as a versatile little word, comparable to our French "chez," capable of expressing both location and relationship.
H3890.emploi: The word appears once in the preserved biblical text (Ezra 4:12). It is used to describe the Jews who left the court of the king of Persia. The preposition marks here the dwelling or previous authority: these Jews came "from the house of" the king, that is, from his court or territory. Its use remains limited in the Hebrew Bible, but the meaning is clear: proximity, dwelling, presence with someone.
H3890.portee: This little word reminds us that presence alongside someone — near an authority, a master, or a friend — shapes our life and actions. The Jews who leave the king's court to rebuild the Temple no longer go "to his house": it is a change of residence that also changes their mission. For the believer, this evokes the importance of seeking the presence of God, of being "at home" with Him.

sens: Deviation, a path that strays from the straight line
Words that deviate from the truth
Twisted or perverse conduct
Deviation from moral uprightness
H3891.detail: 1. In its primary sense, a detour is a path that does not go straight: instead of following the direct route, one strays. 2. Figuratively, it refers to a false or deceptive word, a word that "does not go straight" because it does not tell the truth — it deviates from honesty. In Proverbs 4:24, "the detours" refer to those dishonest words that must be kept far from one's lips. 3. More broadly, it encompasses any conduct that strays from uprightness: a perverse life, actions diverted from their proper use. The word evokes the image of a winding road, which turns and strays from the goal when it should go straight.
H3891.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to turn" or "to deviate." It first describes a physical path that winds instead of moving straight, then applies morally to anything that deviates from uprightness: a lying word, an intention that turns away from good. It is a term that paints the image of a winding, twisted walk.
H3891.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 4:24. It appears in a passage where the wise man gives his son advice on uprightness: he commands him to keep falsehood away from his mouth and to remove the "detours" from his lips. It is thus a deceptive, tortuous word that the young man must reject. The context shows that "detours" opposes the uprightness of speech: one should not speak in a twisted, indirect, or deceitful manner.
H3891.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us of the importance of sincerity in speech. A righteous life begins with a righteous mouth: one should not speak twisted, deceptive, or false words. It is a call to honesty, to truth spoken directly, without artifice or calculation.

sens: Containing moisture, not dry
Alive and vigorous, referring to a plant
New, recently prepared or used
Possessing strength, vigor
H3892.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the word is that of moisture: a green or fresh thing has not lost its water. The fresh cords that the Philistines bring to Delilah (Judges 16:7) are still supple and moist, unlike dry cords that would break. This is why the fresh grapes of Numbers 6:3 are juicy grapes, full of juice.

2. Applied to nature, the word denotes the vitality and vigor of plants. The green tree in Ezekiel 17:24 is one that lives, standing strong, while the dry tree approaches death. The green branches of poplar that Jacob peels in Genesis 30:37 are branches full of life, freshly cut.

3. The word can also qualify what is new or recently made, as fresh opposes old and worn out. A fresh cord has not had time to dry out and lose its suppleness.

4. By extension, fresh and green evoke strength and vigor: one who eats fresh remains vigorous, like the Nazarite of Numbers 6:3 who, by abstaining from wine and grapes, preserves his strength in abstinence.
H3892.origine: The Hebrew root lach evokes the image of moisture and life. It appears only a few times in biblical Hebrew, but it remains linked to the fundamental concept of what has sap, fluidity, youth. The constant contrast in the Bible between green (lach) and dry (yabesh) reflects a cosmic opposition: that between life and death, water and dryness. The green tree is the living tree; the dry tree is a dead or dying tree.
H3892.emploi: The word appears six times in the Bible, always in concrete contexts. In Genesis 30:37 and Ezekiel 17:24, 21:3, it describes living trees or branches, full of sap. In Numbers 6:3, it qualifies the fruits of the grape that are not dried out. In Judges 16:7 and 16:8, it applies to the supple and moist cords with which Samson is bound. In all cases, the word expresses a quality of strength, youth, or vitality in contrast to what is dry, old, or weakened. Samson can only be defeated by fresh cords, never by dried cords.
H3892.portee: This word reminds us that in biblical thought, life is manifested by vitality, suppleness, moisture: what is fresh has resilience and strength. Conversely, drying out means drawing closer to death. For the believer, this evokes the importance of remaining spiritually alive, keeping the freshness of faith in the face of temptations that dry us out and weaken us. God's green tree prospers; man's dry tree will perish.

sens: Physical strength, vital energy of the body
Capacity to act, to accomplish tasks
State of freshness and energy against the passage of time
H3893.detail:
1. Vigor is the raw physical strength that animates the living body. It is the energy and power we feel in our muscles and movements (Deuteronomy 34:7).
2. This vigor is also the concrete ability to do what the body is meant for: to walk, to work, to act. It denotes the faculty of being active and performing.
3. More broadly, vigor is the state of freshness and dynamism in the face of the wear of time. It opposes decline, the weakening that the years naturally bring. In Deuteronomy 34:7, Moses' vigor at one hundred twenty years manifests a miraculously preserved youth: his strength has not abandoned him despite his old age.
H3893.origine: This Hebrew word first designates moisture or freshness (like dew on green grass), then by extension the vitality that keeps the body in its energy. The root expresses the idea of what is fresh, green, living. The image is that of a plant full of sap: it overflows with life and strength.
H3893.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible in Deuteronomy 34:7, to describe the extraordinary state of Moses at the time of his death. At one hundred twenty years, contrary to what one would expect, his vigor has not declined. It is an affirmation of divine protection: God has preserved Moses in an unusual youthfulness until the end of his life.
H3893.portee: This term reminds us that true strength is not that of youth, but that which God grants. The mention of Moses' vigor despite his old age shows that God can sustain His servants beyond natural limits. For the believer, this invites trust in divine strength rather than in fleshly strength.

sens: The internal organs of the body, particularly those of digestion
Figuratively: what is deepest within oneself, the intimate
What fills or delights someone, what nourishes or satisfies them
H3894.detail:
1. The word refers to the internal organs of the belly, especially the intestines. In Job 20:23, it appears in a vision of terror where God fills the belly of the wicked with fire — an image of internal punishment, the verb indicating that God will "satisfy" the guilty not with bread, but with calamity, as if the fire itself had become his food.
2. In ancient thought, the intestines and viscera were seen as the seat of deep emotions and the secrets of the heart. In Zephaniah 1:17, the scattered intestines (translated here as "flesh") represent what is most intimate and vital in the sinner's person, spread out without dignity "like refuse."
3. The word can also metaphorically denote what fills or nourishes someone — hence the translation "trait" in Job 20:23, where the traits of divine anger fill the belly of the guilty like a devastating abundance.
H3894.origine: The Hebrew word לְחוּם comes from a root that evokes the cavity or interior of the body. It is related to other Hebrew terms describing internal space and bodily intimacy. In ancient Hebrew thought, the viscera were not just physical organs, but seats of emotion and will, similar to how we might say "of the heart" or "of the belly" in English.
H3894.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible translated by the Segond, in contexts of divine judgment. In Job 20:23, it features in Bildad's speech about the fate of the wicked: God fills his intestines with fire, an image of internal punishment. In Zephaniah 1:17, on the day of wrath, God spreads the intestines of sinners like dust and refuse — an extreme image of degradation and annihilation. In these two passages, the word emphasizes the intimate aspect of the human body subjected to destruction.
H3894.portee: These two passages remind the reader that sin is not a superficial fault: it wounds the intimate, the vital heart of the person. Divine punishment, if it comes, reaches the man in his depths, not just his outer body but his secret life. It is a call to recognize the seriousness of sin and the relentless justice of God.

sens: The lower part of the face, bony, which holds the lower teeth
By metonymy, the place called Lehi in Judea, the site of a battle involving Samson
H3895G.detail:
1. The jaw refers to the lower bone of the face, where the lower teeth are implanted. This is the concrete and anatomical sense of the Hebrew word. In Judges 15:19, after achieving a spectacular victory by killing a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone, Samson is so thirsty that he cries out to the Lord: God brings forth a spring from the rock, at the place aptly called "the spring of the one who called out" — thus establishing a connection with this makeshift weapon.
2. This same word also designates the site of Lehi in Judea, a strategic location where Samson's battles took place. The name of the place likely comes from its geographical shape (a ridge resembling a jaw) or an ancient tradition. It is a typical example of how a concrete word (the jaw) becomes a place name.
H3895G.origine: The Hebrew word לְחִי (lechi) literally means "jaw" or "cheek." It is related to the root that designates the lateral parts of the face. The same word, written לֶחִי (lechi), is used as a proper noun to designate a place in Judea — showing how an anatomical term could become a geographical landmark in ancient Hebrew language.
H3895G.emploi: This word appears very rarely in the Hebrew Bible. Its main occurrence is in Judges 15:19, in the story of Samson: after his victory over a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone (jawbone in English, but here it refers to the complete bone, the weapon), Samson is exhausted from thirst and asks God for help. The text plays on the meaning of the place (Lehi) and the image of the jaw as a weapon already mentioned. The word thus remains highly associated with this particular narrative and Samson's superhuman strength.
H3895G.portee: This word reminds us how God uses seemingly weak or unexpected means to accomplish His purposes: a simple donkey's jaw, found by chance, becomes a formidable weapon. It is an invitation to see beyond appearances and to trust in God's power rather than conventional means.

sens: Fleshy part of the face, on each side of the face
Jaw, the set of bones in the mouth that hold the teeth
Part of the carcass of a sacrificed animal
H3895H.detail:
1. The cheek is the visible part of the face, between the eye and the mouth. It can be beautiful (Song of Solomon 1:10: "Your cheeks are beautiful") or serve as a target for violence: Job 16:10 describes one who is insulted and struck "on the cheeks," while Isaiah 50:6 speaks of cheeks given to those who pull out the beard. It is a vulnerable and exposed part of the face.
2. The jaw refers to the bone or the set of structures that form the mouth and hold the teeth. In animals, it is distinctive: Deuteronomy 18:3 lists the jaws as a portion due to the priest from the sacrifice. In the case of the crocodile, Ezekiel 29:4 speaks of putting "a hook in your jaws," the image of an animal tamed by a hook passed through its mouth.
3. At meals or when sharing game, the jaw, along with the shoulder and stomach, was the portion reserved for the priest: it was a choice piece, visible and easy to identify on the carcass.
H3895H.origine: The Hebrew word לְחִי (le-chi) designates the area of the jaw and cheek. It comes from a root that refers to the idea of splitting or separation (the jaw divides the face). The word belongs to the vocabulary of the human and animal body, very common in the concrete descriptions of the Hebrew Bible.
H3895H.emploi: The word appears 19 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in contexts of bodily violence, beauty, or sacrifice. The cheeks are associated with the dignity of the face: they can be slapped (1 Kings 22:24: a prophet strikes on the cheeks), spat upon (Isaiah 50:6), or wept over (Lamentations 1:2: the cheeks stream with tears). In sacrifice narratives (Deuteronomy 18:3), the jaw is a coveted piece. In animals — crocodile (Ezekiel 29:4), lion (Job 40:21) — the jaw embodies power or dominance. The place Ramath-Lehi (Judges 15:17) derives its name from the donkey's jaw thrown there by Samson.
H3895H.portee: The cheek and the jaw remind us of the vulnerability of the human body, exposed to violence and humiliation.
