Isaiah 50:6 finds an echo in the Passion of Christ: it is a sign of accepted suffering. Conversely, the beauty of the cheeks in the Song of Solomon celebrates love that honors the body. This word invites respect for the integrity of the face and the person.

sens: Region of Judah where Samson's exploits against the Philistines took place
H3896.detail: 1. Lehi is a region in Judah, likely located in the Shephelah (the hilly area between the coast and the mountains) near the border of the mountainous land of Judah. It is here that Samson, seized by the Spirit of the Lord, performed remarkable feats against the Philistines (Judges 15:14).
H3896.origine: The Hebrew name לֶחִי (lechi) literally means "jaw." According to biblical tradition, this place was named in reference to the event where Samson killed a thousand Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey (not mentioned in the provided usages, but related to the context of the passage). The word refers both to a part of the body and a geographical location, illustrating how the Bible sometimes associates place names with memorable events.
H3896.emploi: Lehi appears three times in the account of Judges 15, all within the story of Samson. The Philistines gather there and extend their troops to this place (Judges 15:9). It is at Lehi that Samson, filled with the Spirit of the Lord, breaks his bonds and acts with power (Judges 15:14). Finally, God splits the rock at Lehi to bring forth water, naming the spring En-Hakkore, which means "spring of the one who cries out" (Judges 15:19). These three occurrences form a coherent narrative of a place marked by extraordinary divine interventions.
H3896.portee: Lehi is the stage where God manifests His power in a spectacular way. It serves as a reminder that seemingly impossible victories become possible when one is filled with the Spirit of God. The spring that gushes from the rock also symbolizes God's care for His people, even amidst battles.

sens: To pass the tongue over something
To absorb or consume entirely
To submit completely, as a sign of humiliation or reverence
H3897.detail:
1. To lick means to pass the tongue over a surface: it is the action that animals take to drink or clean. In 1 Kings 18:38, the fire of the Lord "licks up" (image: licks) the water from the trench, as a tongue would lick a liquid.
2. The verb can also describe how an animal devours or grazes: in Numbers 22:4, Balak fears that the multitude of Israel will "lick up" everything just as an ox grazes on grass — the idea is of complete, progressive, relentless consumption.
3. Figuratively, to lick the dust expresses extreme humiliation and total submission before someone more powerful. In Psalms 72:9 and Isaiah 49:23, the enemies or foreign kings "lick the dust" from the feet of the king of Israel: it is the gesture of the defeated who bows down and acknowledges their defeat. In Micah 7:17, the trembling nations "lick the dust" as a sign of reverential fear before the God of Israel.
H3897.origine: The Hebrew verb לָחַךְ (lachakh) paints a vivid image: that of the tongue licking. It primarily appears in images of submission or total consumption, and is related to roots that describe animal gestures. The Greek Old Testament often translates it with the corresponding Greek verb that retains the same concrete image.
H3897.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible. Its literal sense (to lick) is seen in 1 Kings 18:38 where the fire "licks up" the water. But almost all usages are figurative: in Numbers 22:4, it describes progressive and total consumption; in Psalms 72:9, Isaiah 49:23, and Micah 7:17, it becomes the image of supreme humiliation and submission before God or before the king established by God. These last three passages all use the expression "lick the dust," which symbolizes the complete lowering of the defeated or the rebel.
H3897.portee: This image of licking the dust shows us how the Bible speaks of submission to God: not a cold and distant obedience, but a total, humble capitulation in the face of divine power. It teaches that the nations and enemies of God will ultimately recognize His lordship, even against their will, and that those who hope in Him will ultimately be exalted. It is a promise of victory that comes through the image of the adversary's humiliation.

sens: To engage in physical combat, in a military sense
To wage battle, to go to war between two armed forces
To struggle, to oppose forcefully against someone or something
To resist, to stand firm in a conflict
H3898A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of combat in a physical and military sense: two adversaries or two armies confront each other directly. Exodus 1:10 speaks of the Egyptians fearing that Israel will "fight" against them in case of revolt — it is a threat of direct armed confrontation.
2. The word also designates the battle or military campaign waged by one people against another. Joshua 11:5 recounts how the kings of Canaan gather to "fight" against Israel: it is the collective mobilization for war.
3. By extension, it refers to any resolute opposition, even verbal or strategic. Psalms 109:3 states that the enemies of the psalmist "make war against him without cause" — a persistent hostility, not necessarily a clash of arms.
4. The word can also express resistance, tenacity in the face of an adversary: to hold firm despite the attack.
H3898A.origine: The Hebrew root לחם (la.cham) expresses the idea of combat and confrontation. It has no etymological relation to the word לחם (bread, food), although the consonants are identical: these are two entirely different words. The verb is regularly used in the Qal (simple form) to describe the action of fighting, and in the Niphal (passive or reflexive form) to express engagement in battle or war.
H3898A.emploi: This verb is very frequent in the Hebrew Bible: about 165 occurrences. It first appears in the accounts of Exodus and the desert (Exodus, Numbers), where Israel learns to fight against the Amalekites and the peoples of the desert. It becomes dominant in the conquest narratives of Canaan (Joshua, Judges), where the verb describes the repeated confrontations between Israel and the peoples of the promised land. In the books of Kings and Chronicles, it evokes royal wars, notably those of David and Jeroboam. The Psalms also use it figuratively to express spiritual struggles or verbal hostilities. The context remains that of resolute opposition and engaged confrontation.
H3898A.portee: The word "to fight" reminds the Christian reader that the life of faith is not passivity, but an active struggle. The Old Testament shows Israel battling under God's guidance: the Lord fought with His people. For the Christian, this verb also evokes the spiritual battle taught in the New Testament (Ephesians 6), the necessity to stand firm in the face of adversity and not to retreat in the face of trials. It is an invitation to vigilance and resistance in faith.

sens: To consume food
To devour, consume
To participate in a meal
To appropriate or enjoy something
To adopt an attitude or way of life
H3898B.detail:
1. The primary meaning is simple: to eat is to absorb food for life. In Proverbs 9:5, Wisdom invites: "Come, eat of my bread," a concrete image of sharing.
2. The word can also mean "to consume" or "to devour," as when disease and famine "consume" the people in Deuteronomy 32:24: here, eating takes on a destructive turn, the food destroys instead of nourishing.
3. Eating together means being at the table, as suggested in Proverbs 23:1: "When you sit down to eat with a ruler." It is sharing a meal and presence.
4. To take "part" in a feast (Psalms 141:4) also means to participate in its benefits or life: sharing at the table means associating with the one who welcomes you.
5. More broadly and figuratively, to eat someone's bread or wine means to adopt their way of life or values: "They eat the bread of wickedness" (Proverbs 4:17) means that the wicked feed on wickedness; they live by it.
H3898B.origine: The verb לָחַם (la.cham) comes from a root that evokes the idea of consuming or being consumed. In Hebrew, this verb generally denotes the action of eating. The same root appears in the word לֶחֶם (le.chem), "bread," the main food consumed. The verb is used both for the physical absorption of food and for more figurative usages.
H3898B.emploi: This verb appears six times in the Bible according to the provided usages, mostly in the wisdom books (Proverbs and Psalms) and once in Deuteronomy. In Proverbs, it describes the concrete act of nourishing oneself (Proverbs 9:5) but also of sharing a table with others (Proverbs 23:1, 23:6). The word takes on a moral value: eating the bread of wickedness (Proverbs 4:17) amounts to living according to malice. In Deuteronomy, the verb is used in the passive or past: being "consumed" by disease shows how eating changes the subject — it is no longer the man who eats, but the suffering that devours him. This variation emphasizes that the act of nourishing extends from the biological to the spiritual.
H3898B.portee: This word reminds us that eating is never neutral: it is an act that unites or separates us, that nourishes or corrupts us. By sharing a meal, one accepts a communion. By eating the bread of wickedness, one becomes complicit. For the believer, this sheds light on the meaning of the table — both the Lord's table and the world's — and invites them to discern what truly nourishes them spiritually.

sens: Basic food made from flour and water, baked
Food in general, what is eaten
Subsistence, means of living
What nourishes the soul or spirit
H3899G.detail:
1. Bread in the strict sense is the main food of biblical times: a cake baked from flour and water. It symbolizes the meal and civilization (Genesis 47:12 recounts that Joseph provided bread for all the household of his father).
2. The word also more broadly denotes anything that is eaten, food in general: when Saul forbids his men from taking "food" before the battle (1 Samuel 14:24), he is speaking of all sustenance. Job complains that his appetite refuses food (Job 6:7).
3. By extension, bread becomes subsistence, what allows one to live: giving bread to someone means keeping them alive. He who earns his bread earns his life.
4. The Bible also uses this word in a spiritual or moral sense: bread can represent what nourishes the soul, what sustains inner life.
H3899G.origine: The Hebrew word לחם (léchem) comes from a root that likely means "to fight" or "to wage war" in some ancient contexts, but in biblical usage, it has settled on the meaning of bread and food. The root is attached to the idea of what sustains and allows one to live. Related words also denote fighters or those who wage battle, as an army, like a person, needs bread to survive.
H3899G.emploi: The word appears 67 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in Genesis, Psalms, and Proverbs. It is used first in the literal sense: the bread of sacrifice, the bread of the house. Then it extends to the broader sense of food: in Leviticus 3:16, the fat of the sacrifice is the "food" offered to the Lord. In Proverbs and Job, it takes on a moral flavor: the bread earned honestly (Proverbs 30:8), the bread of the one who works. The prophets use it to evoke hunger and lack (Jeremiah 5:17 announces that the enemy will devour the bread of the land). In historical and narrative passages, it simply marks daily life and relationships (sharing a meal is sharing bread).
H3899G.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader grasp the spiritual density of the biblical narrative. The Bible speaks little of food out of luxury: it does so when it concerns subsistence, dependence on God, or communion among men. When Jesus says, "Man shall not live by bread alone," he takes up this image from the Hebrew Bible: bread nourishes the body, but the soul needs another kind of nourishment. Meditating on this word also reminds us that giving food is a form of biblical love.

sens: Basic food made from flour and water, baked
Food in general, daily sustenance
What sustains physical life
H3899H.detail:
1. Bread is the main food: ground wheat, kneaded and baked. In Genesis 3:19, Adam will eat his bread "by the sweat of his brow" — the labor to produce this grain and transform it into food is at the heart of the human condition. Isaiah 44:15 describes a man who bakes bread with the wood he has cut: an image of bread as the fruit of daily work.
2. The word also denotes food in a broad sense, what sustains. In Psalms 104:15, bread "sustains the heart of man," just as wine gladdens it: it is the vital food that allows one to live and stand. Deuteronomy 8:3 teaches that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God — bread here represents everything that nourishes the body.
3. Sometimes the word simply means subsistence, the means of living. In 1 Samuel 2:36, a man will beg for "a piece of bread" to have something to eat: bread becomes the symbol of the minimum vital, of what one asks for when they have nothing.
H3899H.origine: The Hebrew word lechem comes from an ancient root meaning "to fight" or "to struggle" — the primary idea is that of the struggle for life, the fight to obtain one's food. But the word quickly evoked bread itself, the food earned through this struggle. It is a simple and fundamental word in the daily life of the Hebrews; it has no notable variants in the Bible, as it is always the same bread that nourishes the people, from the desert to the harvests of Egypt.
H3899H.emploi: The word lechem appears more than 206 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Pentateuch and historical narratives — wherever the concrete life of the people is discussed. In the Desert, God sends manna, called "bread from heaven" (Exodus 16:4 and following), to show that it is He who nourishes His people. In the laws of worship, the "showbread" (the twelve loaves on the table of the sanctuary) represents the perpetual offering of the people to God. The word can be very literal (a piece of bread to eat, 1 Samuel 2:36) or more figurative (the subsistence guaranteed by God, Deuteronomy 8:3). Sometimes it also denotes grain standing or the harvest, as bread depends on it (Leviticus 26:5: "you shall eat your bread to the full"). It is a key word for understanding the relationship between human labor and divine providence.
H3899H.portee: Bread teaches the reader that physical life is a gift from God and that it comes through work: it is the dignity of the one who earns their bread. But it also reminds us of our dependence on God — "man does not live by bread alone." When Jesus says in the New Testament, "give us this day our daily bread," he takes up this word and this tension: to recognize that we need physical bread, but that we depend first on God. Thus, bread becomes the symbol of all that sustains us — body, soul, spirit.

sens: daily food, essential sustenance
allocation or income intended to feed someone
food in a broad sense, including meats and other dishes
H3899I.detail:
1. Bread is the primary meaning that comes to mind: the bread of wheat or barley that nourishes. It is the staple food in Israel. But in the Bible, this word also means "food" in general, anything that is eaten. In 1 Kings 4:22, the "provisions" (that is, food) that Solomon consumes each day are mentioned: flour and grains, of course, but the word covers all the necessary foods for his household.
2. The word also refers to an allocation or income paid regularly for living. In Nehemiah 5:14 and 5:18, Nehemiah refuses the "income" of the governor—that is, the provisions and money that the king granted to the one who governed, which he could have lived on. It is a subsistence allowance.
3. In Jeremiah 52:33, Jehoiachin "always ate at the king's table": the word "always" comes from this. The king provided him with his food regularly, an established right. It is assured food, a recognized status.
H3899I.origine: The Hebrew word לֶחֶם (leḥem) comes from a root that means "to fight" or "to struggle," hence the image that bread is what supports the struggle of life, what allows one to survive and act. In ancient Hebrew, this word is very common and primarily refers to bread as the main food, then extends to all food. It has given rise to derived words to speak of one who prepares food, the table, etc.
H3899I.emploi: The word appears five times in our uses, but in biblical Hebrew, it is very frequent. In these five passages, it has a broad meaning: it is not the baker's bread, but food, allocation, income. In 1 Kings, it refers to the daily provisions of the royal palace. In Nehemiah, it is the administrative allocation that the Persian governors received, what was given to them to live on. In Jeremiah, it is the king's table, assured food. The word thus shifts from the concrete (bread, food) to the figurative (maintenance, income, the right to live at someone else's expense).
H3899I.portee: This word reminds us that food is not a trivial matter: it is the means of subsistence, of living, and often a sign of social position or favor granted. By refusing the "income" of the governor, Nehemiah refuses to be supported by the people; he refuses a privilege. It is an act of justice. Bread, throughout the Bible, is linked to the covenant, to dependence on God, and to relationships of love or domination between men.
